# Runtime Parity Closure Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking. **Every task begins with its Pre-check: run the command, compare against the recorded expectation, and STOP and report if reality moved — do not build on a stale premise.**

## Owner decisions 2026-09-01: four answered, and three that were already settled

Asked with the owner's own criterion — *important for the plan and the runtimes* — and weighted toward **maximum parity coverage**. Three candidates were withdrawn before asking, because reading them showed they were not open:

- **P2.306 is REFUTED**, not pending. The deny **is** honoured live, and the fix its own row recommended **would have removed a working credential control**.
- **P3.139 was already decided** under the 2026-08-28 delegation — the fall-through stays off, one flag away, with the numbers recorded. The honest reason is not the latency: the 28-of-28 was measured against a two-line transcript.
- **P6.9 was already deferred** by owner ruling 2026-08-28, in the owner's own words.

That is a controller error worth keeping: **the triage that produced the eight was a regex over row text, not a reading.** Three of eight were stale. A decision queue assembled by pattern-match will present settled questions as open ones, which costs the owner's attention rather than a lane's.

**The four answers:**

| Row | Decision | What decided it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **P4.7** | **Do not build** | It is Pi-only by construction, so building it manufactures a divergence in the wave meant to close them. An honest zero beats a Pi-only one. |
| **P3.242** | **Refuse, naming the override** | The silencing is host-wide, so a named refusal behaves the same on all three; the alternative quietly redefines a file whose name means *local override*. |
| **P2.381** | **Explicitly disable** | Pi and claude have no such transport, so disabling makes all three identical — the divergence disappears rather than being masked. |
| **P3.129** | **Defer, and record it as a posture** | Deferral is a decision; unstated ignorance is not. The note must say our credential floor is evidenced on darwin only. |

**Three of the four are parity-positive in the same direction, and it is worth naming why:** where a capability exists on one runtime and not the others, the owner chose **removal or refusal over selective enablement** every time. That is the *host makes the residual difference uniform or honest* rule applied to product scope rather than to code — and it is cheaper, because a capability not built needs no per-runtime seam.

**Still open and not asked:** `P4.1` and `P4.3` remain paused on playground drafts, which are work rather than answers. `P2.478` is unblocked by the P4.7 ruling and is now a deletion.

## OQ-6 — RESOLVED 2026-08-23: our host gate enforces on all three paths

The owner asked why the permission matcher is not simply "1:1 like Claude". Measured before answering:

- **Claude's implementation is unreadable.** `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk` ships minified bundles
  (`sdk.mjs` 1.26 MB, `bridge.mjs` 1.32 MB); there is no matcher source. AGENTS.md's own rule allows
  paraphrase only from proprietary binaries. So "1:1" is unverifiable by construction — only
  behavioural parity against the documented pages is checkable, which is what this plan does.
- **The SDK does have its own engine** — its types expose `allowedTools`, `disallowedTools`,
  `permissionMode`, `canUseTool`, `PermissionResult`, `permission_denials`.
- **PREMISE CORRECTED (controller error, 2026-08-23) — read this before the resolution below.** My
  first write-up of this OQ said "the SDK is held at `permissionMode: 'bypassPermissions'`, so we
  decide alone". **That was true before R3 and is false today.** R3 removed the bypass. On the claude
  path now: the real permission mode is passed to the SDK
  (`buildClaudePermissionModeOptions(getPermissionMode(sessionKey))`), `settingSources` loads the
  user's `.claude/settings.json`, and **the SDK applies their deny/ask/allow rules itself**. Our gate
  runs as a **layer above** it — a PreToolUse hook whose allow carries `permissionDecision: 'allow'`,
  which "skips the permission prompt" (`hooks.md`), so our approval suppresses the SDK's card without
  switching its system off. `packages/shared/src/agent/claude-agent.ts` symbol `runPreToolUseChecks` does call `runPreToolUseChecks`, so our splitter
  is load-bearing on this path — but the arrangement is **layered, not exclusive**.
- **And the site records the strongest answer to the owner's "why not 1:1" question, from R3's own
  author:** Claude's rules match command **STRINGS**, while our gate parses the command into an
  **AST** (`bash-validator.ts`) — which is how Safe Mode allows a genuinely read-only command and
  refuses one that merely *starts like* an allowed one. Being 1:1 here would be **weaker**, not
  merely different. That is why the bypass existed at all, and R1 is what let it go: our allow now
  carries `permissionDecision: 'allow'`, so an approved read-only command still runs with no card.

**The option, stated fairly:** hand the SDK the rules instead of bypassing it, and the claude path
becomes 1:1 by construction, with our splitter out of it entirely.

**Why it is not obviously a simplification.** It splits the model in two: the SDK's engine on claude,
ours on Pi and codex — where nothing exists to delegate to. Today's uniformity across the three IS
the parity this plan exists to produce; a user switching runtime would start seeing different answers
to the same rule. It also moves a behaviour we currently own and test into a binary we cannot read,
which trades our defects for undiagnosable ones.

**The cheaper simplification, and the one the priority ruling already implies:** match the DOCUMENTED
behaviour rather than the shell's parse, and make the splitter DUMBER, not smarter — fall to
`unparseable` (→ prompt) more eagerly instead of parsing cleverly. Note what that reframing explains:
P2.71's Critical happened precisely because the splitter was made smarter (taught to understand
comments); a dumber splitter that prompted would have been safe.

**RESOLVED by the owner 2026-08-23, on the axis the owner named: cost of MAINTENANCE under constant
upstream churn — Claude, Pi and Codex all keep updating.** Keep the host-side gate authoritative on
all three paths. **Note what the corrected premise above means for this ruling: it confirms the
SHIPPED design rather than changing it.** No code change follows from this decision — the claude path
already layers our gate over an active SDK permission system, which is the arrangement the owner
chose. What the ruling settles is the FUTURE question: do not move rule evaluation into the SDK to
"simplify", and do not read the layering as duplication to be cleaned up.

The decisive argument is that the alternative does not remove our engine, it **adds a second one**:
Pi and codex have nothing to delegate to, and our own additions (protected paths, the removal
breaker, worktree approval, classifier routing) do not exist in the SDK, so they would have to be
re-attached on top of its verdict anyway. After the "simplification" we would maintain two engines.

What breaks on an upstream update, per option:

| Event | Host gate everywhere (chosen) | SDK on the claude path |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| Claude changes DOCUMENTED behaviour | one place to fix; caught by the coverage maps and sentence-anchored citations we already run | two places: the SDK changes itself, and our Pi/codex engine must be pulled to match |
| Claude changes an UNDOCUMENTED internal | does not reach us — we do not use its matcher | the claude path changes **silently**, inside a minified bundle; found from a user report, not a diff |
| SDK version bump | no permission effect | becomes a behaviour-changing release |
| Pi / codex update | no rule engines there — nothing to track | same |

To keep cross-runtime parity under the alternative we would have to **mirror the SDK's changes into
our own engine**, i.e. track an opaque binary in addition to the docs. Strictly more work, not less.
Accepted cost of the chosen option: when Claude changes documented behaviour we must notice and
follow — but that work exists under either option, and the machinery for it already exists.


## OQ-7 — RESOLVED 2026-08-27 from the page: a crash is an artifact, not a cost signal

Surfaced by P2.129, which fixed half its row and refused to force the other half. **This is a
behaviour question with a tested decision on each side, so it is the owner's, not a lane's.**

Measured: a crash turn emits `costReporting: 'unsupported'`; `mergeCostReporting`
(`packages/server-core/src/sessions/SessionManager.ts` symbol `mergeCostReporting`) folds `unsupported` + a later `reported` to **`partial`, permanently**, and
this is **not** crash-first-specific — `unsupported` before or after `reported` both give `partial`.

The axis P2.129 established, and it is a real distinction rather than a hedge:

- **A crash cannot establish "this runtime cannot price."** That was the false, persisted notice, and
  it is fixed.
- **A crash IS evidence that "this session's total is incomplete."** That is what `partial` says, and
  saying it is arguably correct.

So the question is only whether a *first-turn* crash — a session that then runs normally for hours —
should carry `partial` for its whole life. Options:

1. **Keep it.** The total genuinely is incomplete; this is P2.36's decision, separately tested, and
   reversing it costs a tested behaviour for a display nicety.
2. **Scope it.** Fold to `partial` only when the unpriced turn produced *work* — a zeroed crash with no
   output arguably contributes nothing to a total, so nothing is missing from it.

**RESOLVED 2026-08-27. The owner asked what Claude Code does; the page answers it directly, and the
answer is neither option as first drafted.** `agent-sdk/cost-tracking.md`, §"Recover totals after a
session crash", fetched 2026-08-27:

> "When the Claude Code process crashes, it emits a final `error_during_execution` result and exits,
> in single-shot and streaming input mode alike. That result may carry zeroed `usage`,
> `total_cost_usd`, and `modelUsage`, **so recover the call's totals from what arrived before it**."

So upstream treats the zeroed crash result as an **artifact to be recovered around**, not as data —
there is no "partial" concept in their model at all. And our exact case is named: step 1 (take the
previous turn's result) explicitly does not apply when "**The crash happened on the first turn**",
and step 2 says what to do instead:

> "Sum the `usage` on the assistant messages instead, counting each API response once… This gives you
> the main loop's input and cache tokens. **Subagent usage isn't recoverable this way, and neither are
> output tokens or USD cost.**"

**THE RULING AS FIRST WRITTEN (2026-08-27) — and it was WRONG. Kept here as a correction, not
overwritten, because a lane was already executing it when the refutation landed.** It said: fold to
`partial` only when the unpriced turn produced work, decided by whether assistant messages carrying
`usage` arrived for that turn; if none did, nothing was spent and `partial` is a false statement.

**REFUTED 2026-08-27 by P2.129's review, which tested that exact seam and reports it fails for the
same reason as the others, in precisely the case that motivates it.** The page says a crash result
**"may carry zeroed `usage`, `total_cost_usd`, and `modelUsage`"** — *may*, so the zeros are an
artifact, not evidence of no spend. **The step I failed to take: the absence of observed assistant
messages is not evidence of no spend either.** A request can be billed and its response lost with the
process — exactly the case the page calls unrecoverable when its fallback recovers input and cache
tokens and states that "**neither are output tokens or USD cost**". So the criterion asserted
completeness under uncertainty, which is the one thing this cluster exists to prevent.

**THE RULING, CORRECTED: keep the fold. Option 1.** The reviewer's framing is the reason, and it is
sharper than anything in the first draft:

> the notice guard **withholds** an assertion under uncertainty; making the display say `reported`
> would **make** one.

Both were being called "deferral"; they point in opposite directions relative to the honesty
invariant. And the harms differ in kind, measured: the display renders `$6.00 <partialSuffix>` — a
conservative qualifier on a true number — while the notice was a **false sentence**, persisted as a
`level:'warning'` transcript row that survives reload and is never retracted. Only the second was ever
a defect, and `bc2721e5e` fixed it.

**Two corrections to this section's own facts, both measured by the review:**
- **"crash-FIRST" is wrong for the display half.** It is order-independent — crash first, middle or
  last all yield `partial` — and both directions are already pinned by pre-existing tests at
  `packages/shared/src/telemetry/cost-reporting.test.ts:30-31`.
- **"the claude emitter is the only single-point fix" was imprecise.** `packages/server-core/src/sessions/SessionManager.ts` symbol `mergeCostReporting` is a
  second seam, with `event.terminalIsError` and `event.terminalReason` both already read in the same
  block (`:24459`, `:24470`). It does not change the answer — every seam makes the same
  over-assertion — but it should not have been hidden from whoever read this.

This does not reverse **P2.36** — it scopes it to the case its own reasoning describes ("that turn's
cost is genuinely unknown"), which is true exactly when work happened.

**Parity note, stated because it cannot be dodged:** upstream has no aggregate flag like our
`costReporting`, so there is no literal 1:1 here — the parity is of MEANING (a crash zero is not a
measurement), not of mechanism. Cite the two sentences above at the site, with the fetch date.

**A THIRD SENTENCE, surfaced after the correction by the stopped lane and quoted by nobody until
then — it argues the corrected ruling independently.** From the same page, §"Track costs on failed
conversations" (re-fetched and anchor-checked against the rendered page, 2026-08-27):

> "If a conversation fails midway, you still consumed tokens up to the point of failure."

That is the refutation stated by upstream in its own voice: failure does not mean nothing was spent.
Any rule that reads a crash as "nothing to account for" contradicts it.

**Executes as: nothing but a sentence, and it is done.** The fold stays. `packages/shared/src/agent/claude-agent.ts` symbol `buildClaudeMaxBudgetUsdOptions` was
corrected in `cc25737a8` (comment-only) — see P2.228.

## Brief rule (owner question, 2026-08-27): classify the row against the docs BEFORE writing the brief

**Measured when the owner asked whether briefs are written against the official documentation: ZERO of
the seventeen rows worked that session carried a doc citation.** The honest diagnosis is not "we forget to
cite" — it is that **nobody asks whether a doc governs the row**, so a brief inherits whatever the row
note happens to carry, and a row written without a doc check passes that blindness on.

**The rule, from now on, one line of work per brief.** Classify the row's subject:

- **(a) Our own implementation** — command splitters, RPC timeouts, test hygiene, lint wiring, commit
  order. **The docs say nothing.** Say so explicitly in the brief rather than leaving it ambiguous, so the
  lane does not go looking.
- **(b) A behaviour the documentation specifies** — permission modes and rule vocabulary, cost reporting,
  hooks, env vars, protocol methods. **Open the page, quote the SENTENCE, state the fetch date**, and put
  it in the brief. A line number decays; the sentence does not.

**Where to look, and what exists:** Claude's corpus is `code.claude.com/docs/llms.txt` with a coverage map
at `specs/2026-07-31-claude-coverage-map.md`; Codex's is `learn.chatgpt.com/llms.txt`, 139 pages, mapped
at `specs/2026-08-22-codex-coverage-map.md`. **Pi has no external contract at all** — say that plainly
when a row is about Pi, rather than leaving a lane to search for something that does not exist.

**The measured cost of not doing this, from the same session.** Rows P2.213 and P2.251 both turned on
proxy behaviour. The Claude corpus carries **13 pages** matching proxy/network/corporate, and
`env-vars.md` (fetched 2026-08-27) documents the exact mechanism both lanes converged on:

> `NO_PROXY` — "List of domains and IPs to which requests will be directly issued, bypassing proxy"

Nobody looked. Both lanes reached the sanctioned mechanism by **measuring behaviour**, which is stronger
evidence than a citation — so no harm landed, but that was instinct rather than process. Note also what
the page does **not** say: nothing exempts loopback automatically, which is exactly what the measurements
found. **A doc check would have predicted both results in minutes.**

## Owner ruling on the deferred internals (2026-08-23): the splitter gets DUMBER

The 33 finding-born Phase-2 rows are about the accuracy of our shell parse. **The owner ruled that
the splitter should be made dumber, not smarter: anything we are not sure of falls to `unparseable`
→ prompt the user, rather than being parsed cleverly.**

The evidence for it is this plan's own: P2.71's Critical exists *because* the splitter was taught to
understand comments. A splitter that shrugged and prompted would have been safe.

**MEASURED VINDICATION (2026-08-23, P2.71's fix wave — re-review pending, but the numbers are the
point).** The implementer had already built a correct ANSI-C model and measured it green against the
real shell before the ruling arrived, so the comparison is between two *working* implementations, not
between a fix and a stub. Its corrected full-taxonomy sweep:

| | `allow unparseable → match` (a prompt becoming an approval) | `unparseable → …` overall |
| :-- | --: | --: |
| the accurate ANSI-C **model** | **9** | ~1500 |
| the dumb **guard** | **0** | 0 |

**The accurate parser had the strictly larger blast radius.** That is the ruling's whole thesis
turned from an intuition into a measurement, and it should be cited whenever someone proposes making
this splitter cleverer again. The measured cost of
the ruling is near zero — the blast-radius sweep found no command in the repo corpus that any rule
matched via text a dumber splitter would have refused to parse.

**How to triage each of the 33 against this ruling** (do this instead of working them one by one):

1. **Retired** — the row asks for parse accuracy the ruling no longer wants. Close it with its
   measurement recorded and this ruling cited. Most of the family lands here.
2. **Converted** — the row describes a shape we currently parse confidently and wrongly. Do not fix
   the parse; make that shape fall to `unparseable`. Cheaper, and it cannot be wrong in the unsafe
   direction. P2.71's own fix is the template: guard the shape, revert to parent behaviour, prompt.
3. **Kept** — the row is not about parse accuracy at all (a false claim in a comment, a missing test,
   a header that miscounts its own bullets). Those stay as written; they are cheap and they are about
   truth in the record, not about the shell.

**One row is exempt and is not deferred:** P2.71's Critical is a regression this plan introduced —
a command that used to prompt now auto-approves — so it is finished or reverted. Per this ruling its
fix is the **guard**, not the ANSI-C model.

## Owner ruling on budgets (2026-08-24): show the truth, do not fake the number

**Stated by the owner:** the llm-proxy essentially has no budgets; whether a cost figure exists
depends on the API. We only need to SHOW it — **showing 0 (or "unavailable") is fine; what matters is
that the logic and the code exist.**

**Controller measurement that makes this concrete (2026-08-24):**

| runtime | where a cost comes from | what actually arrives |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| claude | the SDK's `total_cost_usd` (`packages/shared/src/agent/backend/claude/event-adapter.ts` symbol `adaptResult`, delta via `takeReportedCostDelta`) | a real figure |
| Pi | pi-ai's OWN pricing table (`backend/pi/event-adapter.ts:513-518`) | **nothing** for a model it has no price for — and the comment at that site says in terms that this is *every Nessy Gateway model* |
| codex | — | **no cost plumbing at all** (`costUsd` occurs 0 times in its adapter) |

**So the real defect is not "the caps differ per runtime" — it is a cap that silently NEVER FIRES**
because no cost ever arrives, while the UI implies the user is under budget. That is the same
fail-open-that-looks-fine shape this plan has been closing all day, and it is exactly what P2.36 names.

**What the budget rows must therefore deliver (and must NOT):**
1. **Honesty over a number.** An unavailable cost reads as *unavailable* (or 0 with its provenance) —
   never as a satisfied budget check. A cap whose input is absent must SAY so, not pass silently.
2. **The logic exists and is exercised** on every runtime, even where the figure is always 0: the
   accounting path, the cap comparison, and the terminal reason must be present and tested, so the
   moment an API starts reporting cost the cap works with no new plumbing.
3. **Provenance is visible.** Where the figure comes from (SDK-reported vs price-table-derived vs
   unavailable) is part of what is shown, because "0" from a missing price and "0" from a free turn
   are different facts.
4. **Do NOT invent a price table** for gateway models to manufacture a number. A fabricated cost is
   worse than an absent one — it would make the cap fire on fiction.

This reframes P2.36 / P2.43 / P2.44 from "make the caps agree" (impossible — the data does not exist)
to "make the absence honest, and the logic ready".

## Owner ruling on external references (2026-08-24): look outward before building inward

**Stated by the owner:** we may consult Pi extensions in the wild — as a reference, or for outright
copying/vendoring — plus the Claude Code and Codex documentation, wherever that simplifies or solves a
task. This widens what a row may reach for; it does not widen what a row may CLAIM.

**Why it matters here.** This plan has twice had a reference settle a question faster than building
would have: the omnigent analysis killed two candidate instruments by measurement (the type-level door,
and a literal port of its own bench that is green because it measures nothing), and the vendored Claude
SDK's shipped binary killed four managed keys that a doc-faithful mapping would have shipped as fake
enforcement. Both times the reference was worth more as *evidence* than as code.

**The rules that still bind, and they are what keep this from becoming copying-by-vibes:**
1. **A reference is evidence, not authority.** Measure its claim against OUR tree before acting on it.
   The omnigent analysis produced five rows, and one of them exists precisely because the reference was
   WRONG for our path (P2.126: we deliberately do the opposite, and the docstring says why).
2. **Vendoring is a supply-chain act.** Record source + license + the commit or version taken, keep the
   quarantine rules, and say in the row what was adapted versus copied — a "nothing is copied verbatim"
   claim that is stronger than the text is itself a defect (P2.134 carries one).
3. **Docs are a contract, and the contract is the SENTENCE.** `AGENTS.md` already binds this: quote the
   sentence with its fetch date, never a line number alone, and check the corpus snapshot. Where a doc
   list is illustrative rather than exhaustive, the shipped artifact wins — P2.7 proved that by pulling
   the real filter out of the Mach-O when the documented key list turned out to be illustrative.
4. **The share-vs-split test still applies.** A reference showing that a runtime HAS a native mechanism
   closes a row by citation only when we have MEASURED that mechanism reaching the same outcome here.

**Where to reach first, by question type:** a runtime's own capability → its docs, then its shipped
binary when the two disagree (the binary has won three times in this plan); an orchestration shape we
lack → Pi extensions and the meta-harness references; a claim about our own behaviour → always our own
tree, never a reference.

## Owner ruling on share-vs-split (2026-08-24): unify what is cheap to unify, split what is expensive

**Stated by the owner 2026-08-24, generalising from Dev-25:** where we can share one implementation
across the runtimes, share it; where we cannot, and sharing would be expensive to MAINTAIN, split and
support each runtime by its own mechanism. This governs how the remaining rows are triaged — and
especially the P5.1/P5.2 sweeps, where dozens of share-or-split calls get made one gap at a time.

**The failure mode this rule must not become.** "Expensive to unify" is an easy excuse for not doing
parity work. Dev-25 was legitimate *not* because unification was costly, but because **claude has a
native mechanism that reaches the same user outcome** — an allow rule returns null above the
moved-class check (`pre-tool-use.ts:2530`, measured). Without that, "split" is not a decision, it is
an unclosed gap wearing a decision's clothes.

**So the test is three questions, in order, and a split needs all three:**

1. **Does the runtime already HAVE a mechanism that reaches the same user-visible outcome?** Name it
   and MEASURE that it works — do not assume from a doc. If the answer is no, this is a gap: write the
   row, do not record a deviation.
2. **Would unifying ADD an engine rather than replace ours?** This is the OQ-6 argument: delegating to
   the SDK would not remove our gate (Pi and codex have nothing to delegate to), it would add a second
   one whose changes arrive silently inside a minified bundle. If unifying means N engines where we had
   one, split.
3. **Is the SAFETY guarantee unaffected?** Some things must stay shared or the guarantee dies. The
   `nonNegotiable` floors are the standing example: `rm` to home/root, worktree approval, protected
   paths are unclearable on EVERY runtime, and no split may fragment them. A shared floor with
   per-runtime adjudication ABOVE it is the shape that satisfies both halves of this rule.

**Three precedents already follow it, and they are the pattern to copy:**
- **OQ-6** — one host-side gate on all three paths; the SDK's own engine stays bypassed. *Shared,
  because the alternative added an engine.*
- **Dev-25 / P2.105** — the guardian classifier stays Pi-only; claude clears with an allow rule, codex
  with its native approval loop. *Split, because each runtime's own mechanism reaches the outcome.*
- **P3.1** — ONE durable permission store (the workspace `permissions.json`), projected into codex's
  execpolicy `rules/` on every home build. *Shared policy, split translation at the edge* — the shape
  to reach for first, because it keeps one source of truth while speaking each runtime's language.

**Corollary for the sweeps:** a 🟨 row is not automatically a build. Ask question 1 first — if the
runtime already reaches the outcome its own way, the row closes by CITING that mechanism (with the
measurement), which is what "cover the surface" means. Only a measured *absence* becomes work.

The distinction that makes it right: Claude's docs specify the **rule vocabulary, the modes, the

already produced two such duplicates on its own. **First pass: 94 of 107.** The `E`/`F` bundle
(context window, sessions/checkpoints/recovery — 13 capabilities) died on an API error and was **owed,
not quietly treated as covered.**

**Re-run completed the same day: 107 of 107, and it produced 8 more NEEDS_ROW — now `P6.53`–`P6.60`.**
Six of the eight (`E1`, `E3`, `E4`, `F2`, `F6`, `F7`) are from the bundle nobody had mapped at all;

**READ THE TWO RUNS' NUMBERS CAREFULLY — they are not comparable, and the trap is mine.** The first

refuted: **I inserted those 52 rows into the tracker BETWEEN the runs**, so the re-run's verification

## Owner ruling 2026-08-28: the ledger's unowned defects get a phase, not a footnote

**Measured, and it is the reason for this ruling.** Of the capability ledger's 107 capabilities,
**only 17 connect to any row in this tracker at all** — and of the absences, only **five** carry the
`PLANNED` reason, which is the reason that means *"a row exists and here it is."* The dominant reason
is `DEFECT` — **67 capabilities** — which the ledger defines as *built wrong or never built, with no
decision behind it.* A defect with no row has no owner, and nothing in this repository would ever
surface it again.

So: **anyone reading this tracker as "the queue" is reading a queue that does not contain most of the
work.** That is not a criticism of the tracker; it is what happens when a ledger is built from the
documentation corpus while a plan grows from findings, and the two never meet. The ledger says so on
its own first page.

**The ruling (owner, 2026-08-28):** those defects are owed, and they live **in the plan**, not only in
the ledger. They are **not** the current queue — the integration-first priority stands, and they are
worked after it, as the input to the verification pass. But they are rows from now on, so they are
counted, sorted, and impossible to lose.

**They take the `P6.x` band.** `P0` is the fast lane, `P2` the Pi↔Claude slice and its findings, `P3`
codex native adoption, `P4` the renderer, `P5` the contract sweep and close-out. A separate band is
the point: *"what is left in phase 3"* has to stay answerable while sixty-odd rows land, and a band
answers it where a flat append does not.

**Three things a `P6` row must carry, each learned the expensive way on this plan:**

1. **Re-measure at HEAD before executing.** The ledger was assembled **without reading this plan**, so
   a `DEFECT` cell can describe something already fixed. That is not hypothetical: the correction pass
   promoted **nine cells** on exactly this basis, and retired one of its own queue rows (P3.34) as a
   duplicate of a defect closed in `d144ce041`. Some `P6` rows will close on measurement alone, and
   that is the cheapest coverage available anywhere in this plan.
2. **A birth tag** — `[doc:claude]` / `[doc:codex]` / `[doc:none]` / `[remote]` — written by whoever
   opens the row, never inferred later by grep. Standing rule since 2026-08-25.
3. **The evidence asymmetry.** For Claude the documentation IS the contract and a page anchor plus the
   verbatim sentence is the strongest evidence obtainable. For codex the SOURCE outranks the page:
   `github.com/openai/codex`, or the shipped binary. A page-shaped fix has now destroyed working
   behaviour **three times** on this plan (P2.306's credential control, P3.30's CA guard, P3.35's
   phantom A3 channel), every time by looking obviously correct.

**What this does NOT license:** opening a `P6` row for a capability whose cell is `—` (no claim).
A no-claim cell is *nobody measured it* — it is a measurement debt, not a defect, and turning it into
a work row would manufacture work from an absence of knowledge. Those become rows only after they
carry a verdict. There are **60** of them.

## Owner question 2026-08-28: the host's unmeasured cells are measured NOW, not deferred

The owner asked when the no-claim cells get resolved, observing that **the host is common to all
runtimes.** That observation is the answer, and it splits the 69 no-claim cells into two piles that do
not belong on the same schedule.

**The 60 runtime cells are blocked on someone else.** They are no-claims for reasons outside our
reach: the codex sweep never probed Pi or Claude for most rows and inferring across would manufacture

the verification pass, where measuring is the work.

**The 9 host cells are blocked on nobody.** There is no vendor, no closed binary, no other team's
corpus — the host is ours, and its column is derived from the switch-safety verdict, so a no-claim
there means **nobody ever asked whether that capability survives a switch.** That is this plan's own
central question, on our own code. Deferring it would be deferring the cheapest measurement available
against the owner's stated goal.

**So they are measured in the current wave.** The nine: `B8` skills from an administrator-owned
location, `D1` being told honestly what a switch costs (its cell holds a correction, not a verdict),
`E2` auto-compaction on a windowless gateway model (**already answered by P3.32 — this one closes on
bookkeeping alone**), `E3` compact-instructions steering, `F3` forking a conversation, `J10`
`web_search` execution, `K4` the cheap/mini model on a ChatGPT-authenticated codex connection, `L9`
turning one skill off without deleting it, `L10` bounding the initial skill list's share of the
context window.

**One thing this measurement must not do:** fill a cell to complete the grid. A no-claim is a null and

## The branching factor, measured 2026-08-28: 2.24 — and the queue cannot converge by closing rows

The owner asked whether finishing the permissions group would make the rest go faster. **Measured over
24 hours: 380 rows opened, 170 closed — 2.24 new rows per closed row, and the ratio did not fall
across the day** (hour 19 alone opened 82). Subtracting the one-off structural addition of 60 rows that
connected the ledger to the tracker leaves **1.9 organic births per closure.** Still above one.

**So no, and the reason matters: branching is a property of FIRST CONTACT, not of permissions.** It was
equally high everywhere attention landed today — the image family gave five rows from one; the
typecheck family turned three packages into five; the managed-env work produced a category the
classifier did not have. **Finishing permissions moves the branching to whatever is looked at next.**
That is not a failure of the audit; it is what an audit does.

**Therefore the queue does not converge by closing rows — arithmetically it cannot at 2.24.** What
converges is **coverage of the governing corpus**, which is the stopping rule already recorded on
2026-08-25, and it *is* moving: the ledger's strongest-evidence marker went from **58 to 81 cells**
today, and the propagated-rather-than-measured share fell with it.

**One correction to scale, so the open count is not read as work:** of 277 open rows, **80 are our own
bookkeeping** — dead citations, drifted counts, stale records — which add nothing for a user and close
in batches; and a further group is the permission-matcher internals the owner has already ruled may
close as *recorded-and-accepted* rather than fixed. **The genuine integration work is roughly a third
of the number.**

**Do not report the open count as remaining effort, and do not promise convergence by closing rows.**

**UPDATE, measured 2026-08-28 late (same method, several windows, so the trend is visible rather than
asserted):** 24 h `2.11` · 12 h `2.49` · 6 h `1.53` · 4 h `1.25` · 3 h `1.17` · 2 h `1.16`. Two honest
readings of that: the fall is **real**, and it is **not yet attributable to the scope filter below** —
the filter went out minutes before the shortest window, while the P6 band's bulk creation sits inside
the long ones and inflates them. The cause most likely is simply that **the big sweeps finished**.

**And the number that matters: anything at or above 1.0 still never closes.** `1.17` is a slower
divergence, not convergence. The queue shrinks only when births fall **below** one per closure, and the
only two levers that do that are (a) the scope filter removing births at the source, and (b) rows
leaving the denominator because they fall outside the goal. Report the ratio with its window; a single
figure with no window has been wrong here twice.


## Owner ruling 2026-08-31: a lane FIXES a small in-zone residue instead of emitting a row

The branching factor above was re-measured on 2026-08-31 from the plan file's own git history —
rows born and rows closed, per day, from snapshots of each day's last commit:

| day | born | closed | born per closed | open backlog |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 08-23 | 79 | 32 | 2.47 | 82 |
| 08-24 | 78 | 52 | 1.50 | 108 |
| 08-25 | 45 | 45 | 1.00 | 108 |
| 08-26 | 29 | 62 | 0.47 | 75 |
| 08-27 | 73 | 35 | 2.09 | 110 |
| 08-28 | 254 | 120 | 2.12 | 244 |
| 08-29 | 153 | 119 | 1.29 | 278 |
| 08-30 | 40 | 55 | 0.73 | 263 |
| 08-31 | 25 | 23 | 1.09 | 265 |

Lifetime: **776 born, 543 closed — 1.43.** So the 2.24 above has fallen to about **1.04 over the last
three days**, which is the good news and also the whole problem: **the open backlog peaked at 278 on
08-29 and is 265 now.** Three days of substantial closing moved it by thirteen. At a branching factor
of 1 the plan does not converge; it circulates.

**One hypothesis was tested and DISCARDED rather than quietly used:** that remaining rows are smaller
than closed ones, on a median note length of 2389 characters closed against 812 open. That comparison
is **confounded** — closing a row appends the lane's report to its own note, so the closed figure is
inflated by the act of closing. There is no valid size measurement, and the argument is withdrawn.

**What the backlog IS made of, measured:** 147 of 237 open rows (**62%**) are residues of completed
work rather than undiscovered gaps, and **73 need an owner decision** — 31% of the queue that no amount
of parallelism can touch.

**The ruling (owner, chat, 2026-08-31).** A lane may **fix a residue in place instead of opening a row**
when all three hold:

1. the file is **already in that lane's zone**;
2. the fix is **under roughly 30 lines**;
3. it changes **no contract and no product posture** — no wire shape, no permission outcome, no
   user-visible policy, nothing an owner would want to decide.

Otherwise — out of zone, larger, or a decision — it stays a row.

**The transparency half is not optional, and it is what preserves the rule this amends.** The standing
rule *findings become plan rows at confirmation* exists so that nothing found is lost. Its **purpose**
is retained and only its **mechanism** relaxed: a lane taking an in-place fix must **list it in its
report and in the commit body**, so the closed row's note carries it and the plan remains a true map of
what was found. **An in-place fix that goes unmentioned is strictly worse than the row it replaced** —
it converts a tracked residue into an untracked change, which is this fork's largest defect class
wearing the costume of efficiency.

**Why the threshold is a judgement and not a lint:** thirty lines is a shape, not a measurement. The
real test is whether the next reader would be surprised to find the change inside that commit. If yes,
it wanted a row.

**Expected effect, stated so it can be falsified:** if the branching factor settles near 0.5, the
remaining lane-closable work is roughly `N/(1-r)` ≈ 360 closures; near 0.3 it is ≈ 260. At the recent
rate of 23–55 closures a day that is two to three weeks, and **the 73 owner-decision rows are the
larger lever** — a single decision session moves the queue further than a wave of ten agents. Re-measure
this table before trusting any of it: every number here is a reading with a date.

## Owner ruling 2026-08-28: the goal is the AGENT LOOP, and four states replace two

The owner narrowed the goal to four statements, verbatim in substance:

1. **Maximally correct runtime switching** between pi, claude and codex.
2. The **host as thin as possible** across all three.
3. **claude and codex used as agent runtimes**, for work as an agentic system.
4. **Pi built strictly to Claude's documentation.**

And the exclusion: *we do not need to support or adapt absolutely everything — only the work of the
agents. We do not need their authorization commands. Working with our endpoint we use dp authorization.
We do not need features unrelated to the agent loop.*

**The filter — a finding becomes a row only if ANY of these holds:**

1. a tool call passes through it;
2. it changes what the model is **told, sees, or may do**;
3. it **differs between runtimes at a switch** (goal 1 — then it qualifies whatever its category).

A finding that fails all three is still **recorded**, under a lane report's `## Out of scope` heading
with its reason. Never silently dropped: an unrecorded finding is worse than an out-of-scope one.

**Two things stay IN however they look:** a control that **silently stops controlling** (this fork's
largest defect class), and anything that differs across runtimes at a switch.

**Four states, not two** — because two states forced three wrong answers on the day this was written:

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `IN` | serves one of the four goals |
| `OUT` | does not — with the reason recorded |
| `GATED` | **built and hidden behind a build flag**, to be re-opened later. Owner on the subscription/provider cards: *«это можно сделать но скрыть… Мы позже откроем»*. Keep it working; do not spend on it; **do not delete it** — filing a gated feature as `OUT` invites someone to remove code the owner intends to re-open. |
| `DEFERRED-LAST` | the owner has ruled on **priority**, not on the finding. The measurement stands. Apply only where the owner actually ruled — never on a lane's own judgement. |

**The controller got this wrong three times in one hour, all the same way: it used a section's CATEGORY
LABEL as the test.** Recorded because the corrections are more instructive than the rule:

- **Corporate launcher** — filed `OUT` as "corporate infrastructure". Wrong: **every Bash tool call
  passes through a launcher seam**, so criterion 1 holds. (The owner then ruled it `DEFERRED-LAST` on
  priority — a different judgement, and theirs to make. See P6.9.)
- **Session surfaces** — three capabilities lumped as "session UI". Wrong twice over: browsing past
  sessions is a **decision already made** (the host store is the single source across all three, codex's
  own thread store stays empty — that is goal 2 working), while *see what is running, attach, stop* is
  squarely `IN`, because **you cannot operate an agentic system you cannot observe or stop**.
- **Subscription cards** — filed `OUT`. Wrong: they are `GATED`, already built behind flags that
  default off.

**The rule, restated: the category decides nothing. The three criteria and the row's own NOTE decide —
and where a row's title suggests one answer and its note another, the note wins.**

The classification lane found five places where the four goals disagree with the code. Three needed the

раз»* — as an analysis pass against that plan, to see what needs supplementing. So: not a column, not

## Owner directive 2026-08-29: the SDK upgrade is owed, and it must run on a QUIET TREE

Owner on `P3.223`: *«обновиться нужно будет и покрыть/убрать разницу если есть в SDK»*. So the upgrade
from `0.3.223` to Artifactory's `0.3.233` is **not optional and not merely a version bump** — the
deliverable is *the difference covered or removed*, which means every host mechanism that duplicates
something the newer bundle now provides natively must be reconciled with it, native-first.

**The known instance, measured: the `archive` plugin source.** 0.3.233 declares it with a **SHA-256
digest** field — *"every download is verified"* — while `P6.39` has just implemented the credentialed
archive download **host-side, without digest verification**, precisely because the vendored bundle did
not offer it. That reconciliation is the shape of the whole task, and there will be others across ten
versions.

**Sequencing constraint, and it is the reason this row is not dispatched immediately:** a version bump
rewrites `node_modules` and the lockfile — a whole-tree change that collides with **every** concurrently
running lane, none of which could then trust its own test evidence. It also lands in the permission
classifier, hooks and tool surfaces, where this plan's most delicate measurements live. **Run it at a
boundary with no other lane in flight**, re-run the affected measurements after, and treat any behaviour
that moves as a finding rather than as noise.


## Continuation protocol (written 2026-08-28): what a fresh controller needs that is NOT in the rows

Owner question: *"can another agent pick this plan up and continue it?"* The rows and their evidence
are self-carrying — this section is the part that was only ever in a controller's head, written down so
the answer is yes. Read `AGENTS.md` first; it is binding and carries the measured traps.

**1. The tracker is the state, and it is edited by ONE writer.** Lanes commit code; the controller pins
rows. A lane that edits the tracker races the sort. Pin with cell-index Python, never a text
substitution — a note cell contains pipes inside backticks and a regex over `|` will corrupt the row:

```python
import re
S = re.compile(r'(?<!\\)\|')                      # a pipe not preceded by a backslash
i = [k for k, l in enumerate(lines) if l.startswith('| P3.30 |')][0]
c = S.split(lines[i]); c[3] = ' ✅ '; c[4] = ' `<sha>` '
c[5] = c[5].rstrip().rstrip('|').rstrip() + ' ' + note + ' '
out = '|'.join(c); lines[i] = out if out.rstrip().endswith('|') else out.rstrip() + ' |'
```

The trailing-pipe guard is not decoration: a row template without it produced **69 malformed rows** that
every parser silently mis-read.

**2. `python3 scripts/sort-plan-tracker.py <plan>` — run it in the FOREGROUND, always.** Backgrounding
it once cost **four pinned rows**: it read the file, sorted, and wrote back over the foreground edits.
It hashes the row multiset and refuses to write if content changed, so it cannot corrupt a row while
reordering — but it cannot see an edit that lands after its read. A new row is inserted **in sorted
position, never appended** (global owner rule): a tracker ordered by when rows were born cannot answer
*what is left in phase 2*.

**3. `python3 scripts/plan-status.py`** prints the per-runtime ledger cut, the tracker counter, the
**ledger-age stamp** (when the ledger was last read, and how many code commits have landed since), and a
**lost-pin invariant** — a row whose note names a commit while its sha cell is empty. That invariant has
fired **five times** and each time it was a real loss, not a false alarm. Run it after every pinning
pass; an empty invariant line is part of the evidence that the pass completed.

**4. Zones are BY FILE, and the reason is a git trap, not tidiness.** `git commit <pathspec>` takes the
file's **working-tree** state, not your hunks — so two lanes holding one file commit each other's
half-finished work. One file, one lane; two rows needing one file run in sequence. Every brief must name
the zone in both directions: *yours*, and *explicitly NOT yours, because another lane holds it right
now*. A lane that finds it needs a foreign file must **stop and report**, not edit — that happened this
day and the lane was right to stop.

**5. A lane brief carries six things**, and omitting any one has cost a measured error here: the row
IDs (the lane reads the full note itself — never paraphrase a row into a brief, a propagated function
name that did not exist cost a whole dispatch); the **evidence rules** (Claude — page anchor plus the
verbatim sentence, `https://code.claude.com/docs/en/<page>.md#<section>`, anchors read off the rendered
page; codex — source at tag `rust-v0.148.0` or the shipped binary is **strong**, a docs page alone is
**weak, intent not behaviour**); the **zone**, both directions; the **traps** that bite in that zone;
the **scope filter** above; and the deliverable, including that a **measured refutation is a first-class
result** — four of them have prevented shipping harm on this plan.

**6. Findings become rows AT CONFIRMATION** (global owner rule), filtered by the three criteria. Rows
are not held as candidates outside the plan.

**7. The ledger (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-28-capability-ledger.md`) is accounting and it batches
at boundaries**, not continuously. One caution outranks the rest when reading it: **57 cells assert
`absent` on a `ᵏ` (code-probe) marker, and that class is systematically biased toward FALSE absence** —
a `ᵏ` verdict is reached by searching for an identifier, and an implementation that achieves the
behaviour structurally rather than by name cannot contain the string searched for. One such cell was
measured wrong and refuted a plan row (P3.75). Never quote a `ᵏ absent` cell as an established gap.

**8. Lane reports go to files, not into the controller's context**, under the session scratchpad; the
lane returns only status, shas, one-line test evidence, and new findings. A controller that pastes
reports into its own context stops being able to hold the plan.

## Priority sharpened 2026-08-28: "permissions" is not one bucket, and only one third of it defers

The owner asked whether the permissions group — the largest open group, 63 rows — can wait until the
integration work is done. **Measured, it cannot be deferred as a label, because three different kinds
of work share it.**

**(1) Live shipped holes — do not defer.** A user is exposed to these now: a newline in a quoted
argument slips past **every** glob rule *including deny* (P2.329); a managed deny lock misses a path
with a newline (P2.344); built-in dp MCP records are appended **after** the filter and escape the
denylist (P2.368); more than 512 permission entries **collapses the whole layer** (P2.269); one command
in seven has the breaker as its only floor (P2.312); and our own allow-rule projection **turns the
sandbox off** for that prefix (P3.80). **This is the owner's own carve-out from the integration-first
ruling — "a shipped security/permission boundary currently wrong" — and it is small.**

**(2) Integration wearing a permissions label — cannot be separated.** The `Read`-deny binding Edit and
Write, whose fix site is the **shared** evaluator rather than one runtime's path (P3.75); codex's cell
after the floor mirror (P3.77); the isolated reviewer on claude (P3.86); the search-results half that
**codex closes and the SDK does not** (P3.105/P3.174/P3.175); the classifier receipt (P3.97). **These
are "give the user every runtime's capabilities through one host" with a different noun in the title.**
Deferring the label would cut the integration work in half.

**(3) Permission-matcher internals — DEFER, and this was already ruled.** The 2026-08-23 owner priority
decision says exactly this: *"the permission matcher's internals are LAST … and several of them may be
worth closing as recorded-and-accepted rather than fixed once the parity work is done."* Sixty-two bare
true-assertions, the PowerShell subprocess cost, two classifiers reading one file oppositely, a
not-zeroed fixture. **The standing ruling has simply been applied more weakly than it says.** Apply it
at full strength: these are not scheduled, and each is a candidate for recorded-and-accepted.

**So the answer to the question as asked is no — and the answer to what it wanted is yes.** The third
kind frees roughly the capacity the owner had in mind; the first two are the plan.

## Owner delegation 2026-08-28: decide from the documentation; where it is silent, be TRANSPARENT and SIMPLE

*"Lean on Claude's or codex's documentation and make the decision yourself. If it is not in the
documentation — then do it as transparently and as simply as possible, so it can be finished later if
need be."*

**This delegates the decision and constrains it, and the constraint is the useful half.** The ordering
is unchanged — the nearest documented solution first — but where the documentation is silent, the
controller now decides rather than queueing, **under two conditions that are not stylistic**:

**TRANSPARENT.** The behaviour must be visible to whoever meets it — the user in a diagnostic, the
operator in a setting, the next lane in a comment naming what was chosen and why. **An undocumented
choice that nobody can see is indistinguishable from a defect**, and this plan has met that shape
repeatedly: a floor inert on one runtime, a warning that stopped firing, a mechanism enabled and never
configured. Each was silent, not wrong-looking.

**SIMPLE.** Prefer the smallest thing that is honest over the most complete thing that is clever —
because *"so it can be finished later"* only holds if the next person can see the whole of what was
done. A narrow mechanism with a stated residue is finishable; a broad one with hidden assumptions is
not.

**What this does NOT license.** It is not permission to invent where the documentation *does* speak —
the read-don't-invent ordering stands above it, and four measured cases on this plan show an invented
answer destroying working behaviour. And it is not permission to decide a **product posture** silently:
where a choice changes what the product *is* rather than how a gap is filled — a user-visible policy,
a safety trade, a cost the operator pays — the transparent form of that decision is still to state it
and continue, not to bury it in a commit.

**Three decisions taken under this delegation today, each recorded in its row:** P3.184 (an OS-enforced
deny is the runtime's own documented mechanism — keep it, make the refusal legible), P3.176 (the page
names the non-deprecated field and `defer`; land those, do not land auto-approve), and P3.139 (the
documentation does not decide a latency/cost trade — leave the fall-through off, keep it one flag away,
and record the measured numbers where the next reader will find them).

## Owner ruling 2026-08-28: when a row is unclear, the answer is READ, not INVENT

Stated by the owner as a standing rule for every row, not a comment on one. **When you do not
understand a task or a row: read the documentation and read the code. You may bring options to the
owner — but the best answer is the one closest to the runtime's own documentation.** Pi is built to
Claude's documentation, so Pi's answer comes from Claude's pages; codex's answer comes from codex. And
we hold references — use them.

**This is a priority ordering, not a menu.** Strongest to weakest:

1. **The nearest documented solution** — what the runtime that owns the surface already specifies.
   Take it, adapted to our shape.
2. **A reference implementation** — `github.com/openai/codex`, `github.com/openai/plugins`' 180 real
   manifests, the Pi extensions, omnigent. Evidence, not authority (owner, 2026-08-24), and practice
   disagrees with spec often enough that reading both is the point.
3. **Ask the owner**, with the options and what distinguishes them.
4. **Invent a value or a mechanism.** Last, and only with the reason written down.

**Why the ordering is this strict, measured on this plan and all of it recent:**

- **P3.32** declined to invent a default context window for unknown gateway models — inventing one
  contradicts the fetcher's own written decision, and a too-generous value **reproduces the bug it
  fixes.** It shipped a loud warning and brought the question here. The owner then supplied tier 1
  directly: **llm-proxy already publishes the real value** (now P3.50). The invented number was never
  needed; nobody had looked at who already knew the answer.
- **P3.30**'s obvious fix would have **deleted a working control** — `CODEX_CA_CERTIFICATE` outranks
  `SSL_CERT_FILE` inside one bundle, so writing ours unconditionally overwrites an operator's own trust
  material. Only reading `codex-rs/http-client/src/custom_ca.rs` showed that.
- **P3.35** found the ledger had named a `base_instructions` channel that **exists in no source file**,
  and the parameter it resembles would have replaced codex's 20,751-character prompt with our 68.
- **P2.306**'s recommended fix would have removed a working credential control.

Four for four: every time a plausible-looking answer was reached without reading the source or the
page, it would have destroyed something that worked. **The failure mode is not being wrong — it is
being wrong in a way that looks obviously right**, which is exactly what an invented answer looks
like.

**The corollary, and it is not optional:** *"I could not find it documented"* is a finding to record,
not a licence to invent. Write what you searched — the page, the anchor, the source file, the
reference — and let the row carry the null, the same way the capability ledger carries `—`.

## Owner ruling 2026-08-28: the LEDGER is accounting, and it batches too

*"Maybe we do another hundred tasks and update it then?"* — and the answer is yes, on the same
reasoning the owner gave for sweeps.

**The ledger is a measure, not work.** Correcting it produces no capability; it makes an existing one
legible. And **reconstruction does not get more expensive with time**, because the tracker rows carry
the commit and the measured evidence in their notes — the rows do the remembering. Reading 136 commits
in a month costs about what reading 36 costs today.

**Measured, which is why the rule is needed:** the last ledger correction landed at 15:30 and **36
code commits landed on top of it within four hours.** A lane correcting the ledger is therefore stale
before it finishes, by construction — the correction runs in one file while eight lanes close rows in
others. **That is not sloppiness; it is what parallel execution costs, and it is permanent.**

**So: the ledger is corrected at a boundary** — before the verification pass, at a close-out, or when
the owner asks for a figure they will act on. Not after every wave.

**The direction of the drift is the dangerous part.** Lanes close defects, so an uncorrected ledger
reports **less coverage than exists**. An understated number is *more* plausible than an overstated
one, so nobody challenges it. A stale cell and a fresh cell are visually identical.

**Therefore the reporting rule, which is the other half and is not optional:** every coverage figure
shown to the owner carries **the date of the last ledger read and the number of code commits landed
since**. The number without its age is the actual defect — the controller reported that table all day
as though it were current, and it was not.

## Owner ruling 2026-08-28: a SWEEP runs at a boundary, not continuously

The owner, stopping a sweep mid-flight: *"I think we run the workflow after we have finished
everything in the plan, so that every item can be checked and reconciled, and only then extended. When
do these sweep workflows run at all? Not every time — that way we eat the budget and build nothing."*

**Correct, and it names a failure mode the controller was walking into.** The distinction:

| | What it produces | What it costs |
| :-- | :-- | :-- |
| **A lane** | code, and findings as a by-product | one agent, scoped by file |
| **A sweep** | rows — questions nobody had asked | 8–16 agents, and its output JOINS the queue |

**So a sweep run while the queue is long buys a question whose answer lands in a queue that cannot
absorb it.** With 250+ open rows, another sixty findings is not progress; it is the appearance of
progress, and it displaces the execution that would shorten the queue.

**The rule: a sweep runs at a boundary.** Specifically — (1) before the verification pass, where its
whole purpose is to reconcile every item; (2) when a NEW governing rule lands and nobody knows how
much it changes (that is what justified the native-first sweep's first run — the rule was hours old);
(3) when a corpus input moves under us, since coverage claims are then stale by construction. **Not on
a schedule, not after every wave, and never as a way to feel productive between lanes.**

**Two sweeps ran today and both were justified, which is why the rule needs stating rather than
assuming.** The ledger→tracker mapping was **structural**: only 17 of 107 capabilities connected to any
row, so the tracker was not the queue and no amount of lane work would have revealed that. The
native-first sweep followed an owner rule stated the same afternoon. **Neither justification recurs**,
so the next sweep waits for a boundary. The stopped run's script is preserved and resumable — the work
is deferred, not discarded.

**Size limit, owner, same day: 6–8 agents.** *"If it is needed, run it — but capped at six to eight agents so we do not overrun; we are checking against the documentation and the code."* Today's two sweeps ran 16 and 8. **The cap is not only budget — it is fit for purpose:** a sweep whose job is to read pages and source carefully does that better in seven deep passes than in sixteen shallow ones, and its output has to be read by one controller either way. Bundle the subject areas to fit the cap rather than splitting the cap across every group.

## Owner ruling 2026-08-28: carry the modality faithfully, let the ENDPOINT refuse

Stated after the image family closed: *"it matters that we support it, but models will not all have
every modality, so it is fine that after a switch a model cannot accept one — it will say so itself."*

**This is the native-first rule applied to capabilities, and it deletes work rather than adding it.**
The host's job is a **faithful translation**, not a capability oracle. We do not gate a modality on our
own guess about what a model can take; we send it in the shape the endpoint documents and let the
endpoint answer. Measured, that is exactly what happens: the gateway **parses** the standard image part
and refuses on model capability with its own named error, identically across both served models, both
roles, stream and non-stream, both URL kinds — while a BYO vision-capable upstream simply works.

**What this settles, and it is more than one row.** Every hardcoded `supportsImages` default is a guess
standing in for an answer the endpoint already gives. So the resolution for `P3.101` and `P3.125` is not
*a better default* — it is **less gating**: prefer the endpoint's refusal to our prediction of it, and
keep a local capability flag only where an explicit per-model declaration exists to honour. That also
dissolves `P3.125`'s live consequence: a BYO `claude-runtime` on a vision-capable upstream stops being
denied a capability that works, because nothing of ours is denying it.

**Two conditions the ruling depends on, and both must stay true.**

1. **The refusal must remain LEGIBLE.** *"The model will say so itself"* holds only while the endpoint's
   answer reaches the user as something they can act on. Today it does — a named 400 naming the part and
   the reason. **If a future path swallows that into a generic failure, this ruling silently becomes the
   silent-loss defect it replaced.** Pin the legibility, not just the transport.
2. **Faithful means faithful.** The two defects behind this were not refusals — they were a **silent
   drop** and a **corruption** (a picture delivered as base64 quoted as prose). Neither would have been
   fixed by better capability detection, and neither is covered by "the model will say so".

**What it downgrades rather than closes.** `P3.127` (the refusal is coarse — the whole turn fails with
the gateway's error string) and `P3.115` (read codex's per-model `inputModalities` for a pre-send
answer) are now **UX improvements, not correctness gaps**: grey-out-and-explain is better than
send-and-fail, and neither is owed for the behaviour to be right. `P3.126` (audio) inherits the same
posture — carry it faithfully when carried at all, and let the endpoint refuse.

## Owner architecture ruling 2026-08-28: NATIVE-FIRST, and the host is the smooth seam

Stated by the owner as a general principle, not a comment on one row: **"this is how it should be
everywhere — the host covers the common usage so switching is smooth."** It governs every open row and
it re-frames what this plan is building.

**The ordering.** For any capability, in order:

1. **Does the runtime already have its own mechanism?** If yes, ENABLE and CONFIGURE it. We supply the
   model; the runtime runs its own machinery. This is the read-don't-invent rule applied to
   architecture, and it is already proven twice: `P3.2` enabled codex's own
   `approvals_reviewer="auto_review"` rather than porting our judge, and `P3.1` projects durable grants
   into codex's own execpolicy rather than re-implementing a gate beside it.
2. **Can the host supply it uniformly for all three?** Then do that once, in the host, not three times.
3. **Only then build it per runtime**, and record why the first two failed.

**THE SECOND HALF, WITHOUT WHICH THE RULE BACKFIRES.** Native-first means three runtimes each doing
the thing their own way — which is *precisely* the switch-safety problem this plan exists to fix. So the
host's job is not merely glue: **the host makes the residual difference either UNIFORM or HONEST.**
Left alone, "let each runtime do its own" manufactures the `SILENT` class — behaviour changing across a
switch with no diagnostic anywhere, which is **53 capabilities today** and the single largest defect
class in the ledger. A native mechanism adopted without a switch verdict is not a closed row; it is a
new silent divergence with a nicer provenance.

**What this changes in how rows are read.** An `absent` cell is now TWO questions, not one: *is the
capability missing*, and *is it missing because the runtime cannot do it, or because we never enabled
what it already has?* Those have completely different costs — configuration versus construction — and
the ledger's `Why` column does not currently distinguish them. **Any row proposing to BUILD something
must first state what it found when it asked whether the runtime already has it.** "I did not check"
is not an answer; "checked, it has none, here is the probe" is.

**What it does NOT license.** It does not license adopting a native mechanism whose behaviour we cannot
observe. The guardian question is the live example: a judge inside the SDK that we can enable but whose
verdicts never reach us **cannot mint a receipt**, and an unauditable second influence on permission
outcomes is worse than an absent one in a bank deployment. **Observability is part of "does it have a
mechanism", not a separate nice-to-have.** Nor does it license weakening a floor: where our own
deterministic gate is stricter than the runtime's native one, the strict one stays and the native one is
defence in depth.

## Owner decisions 2026-08-28: the six open questions, answered

Answered in one pass so execution can continue autonomously. Numbering is the owner's.

**1. The guardian judge — REFRAMED BY THE OWNER, and the reframing is better than any option offered.**
The question put was *which of our three fallbacks*. The owner asked a fourth thing: *"if the Claude SDK
and the codex binary have a mechanism of their own, can the runtime run it — we give them the model and
build an adapter only if we need one?"* **That is the read-don't-invent ordering applied to a safety
feature, and it is already proven on codex:** `P3.2` (`384e2fb38` + `7736e32a9`) enabled **codex's own**
`approvals_reviewer="auto_review"` with an `[auto_review].policy`, surfaced its three guardian
notifications, and added a codex-local denial breaker plus `/approve`. **Codex already judges itself and
we configured it — the codex half of A1 is answered and was answered months ago.** The open half is
Claude, and it is being MEASURED (lane r9): does the SDK carry a mechanism we can enable, can our model
drive it, and — the half that decides everything — **are its verdicts observable enough to mint a
receipt?** A judge whose verdicts we cannot see is a different feature, not an answer. **Owner's
standing instruction: if the answer is no, take option (в)** — leave it Pi-only and say so honestly at
switch time.

**2. The codex pre-tool gate — (a), narrow, and NOT recorded as closing A2.** Confirmed by the owner.
`P3.59` stays closed-by-measurement with its structural reason; option (b) (`untrusted`) is **refused**:
it would make codex prompt on every call and destroy the autonomous mode's value. **P3.81 — assert no
`configWarning` after `buildCodexHome` — is sequenced FIRST**, because it protects the floors that
already exist rather than widening the ones that do not.

**3. Rewind — keep ours; do NOT adopt the SDK's semantics.** Confirmed. The SDK in question is the
**Claude Agent SDK** (`rewindFiles(userMessageId)`), i.e. the claude-runtime path only; codex and Pi
have no equivalent. Adopting it would be a **downgrade**: it restores every tracked file to one
user-message UUID and leaves the conversation untouched, where ours reverts per checkpoint and truncates
the conversation. The nearest documented solution is not always the better one — this is the case where
ours does more, and the rule says read it before choosing, not choose it. **What follows: gate the
affordance where it cannot restore** — same anti-pattern as `/subtask` and `/workflow-name` in the menu
(P3.71, P2.279).

**4. The image across a switch — measure with one packaged live run before building.** Confirmed.
**Scope clarified for the record, because the row's title invites the wrong reading:** this is NOT about
whether a runtime supports images in chat — Claude does, Pi does, and `tools-reference.md#read-tool-behavior`
says so verbatim (*"Images: PNG, JPG, and other image formats are returned as visual content that Claude
can see, not as raw bytes"*). It is about **an image already in a session's history surviving the handoff
to a different runtime.** Today it does not cross as an image on any runtime; `P3.54` made that loss
honest and recoverable. Pi's blocker is **our own** type narrowing; Claude's is **absence of evidence** —
zero image blocks across 217 vendor transcripts, and our verifier cannot distinguish an SDK rejection
from a malformed file, so a wrong guess resumes an empty session silently.

**5. Credential read floor — the owner's premise needs one correction, and it changes the answer.**
The owner wrote *"we do not enable isolation, so effectively everything is available to the agent."*
**Measured: not so.** `deniedPaths` is enforced at the **permission layer**, not the sandbox —
`mode-manager.ts:336` via `matchesDeniedPath`, refusing with *"Sensitive path blocked: <tool> attempted
to access <path>"*. It bites with isolation off, which is exactly why P3.73's lane called it *the only
read-side credential protection a default install has.* So this is a **live, working control that is
merely narrow**, not a dead one. **Owner also states `dp_auth_creds.json` is being reworked under its own
plan** — so `P3.76` splits: the four paths that rework does not touch (`~/.config/gh/hosts.yml`,
`~/Library/Keychains/*`, `~/.docker/contexts/**`, project `.netrc`) proceed now; our own credential file's
pattern lands with that rework, whose owner should be told the floor is waiting on it.

**6. `DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC` — keep as is.** Confirmed. `P3.52` closes as
**recorded-and-accepted**: the asymmetry is deliberate — on the gateway path we control the endpoint and
egress hygiene is the argument; on the subscription path the user has deliberately chosen an Anthropic
account and silencing their updates would be presumptuous. **One check still owed before this is fully
discharged:** whether the flag disables Remote Control on the gateway path. If it does, the cost is
higher than the estimate this decision rests on and the decision should be revisited — that check is not
optional, it is the condition on the answer.

Executes as row P2.21. All other non-negotiables stay refused in plan.

Rationale accepted: the absolute spelling already denied, so literal makes behaviour uniform rather than stricter-in-a-new-place; the cost is one spelling of a build-clean with three working alternatives (`Remove-Item -Recurse ./build`, `./build/*.o`, `Get-ChildItem ./build | Remove-Item`). Reasons of record: sessions ARE the owners, so that tier has no second gate a floor could fall back on; the population is the `packages/shared/src/workspaces/service.ts:1145-1147` manual-repair state where the data may still be wanted; and T13a's single-predicate justification (a vendor transcript is DERIVED and regenerable from the session JSONL) survives only while the sessions do.
