Consequence for scheduling: P4.1, P4.2, P4.3, P4.7 and P4.10 are PARKED until the phase-2/3 rows they render are closed — they are NOT waiting on a sketch from the owner, they are waiting on their own data (since 2026-09-04 a parked-for-data row reads ⬜ with the reason in its note; ⏸ is reserved for rows awaiting an owner answer — P3.362). The extension rows (P4.4, P4.5, P4.6, P4.8, P4.9) are not affected and run in the ordinary queue. Playground discipline applies as always: sweep ALL playground states for any design change, extend the canonical entries with knobs for new states.

- **DR-1 — Pi runtime inspector: RESOLVED 2026-08-22 — BUILD.** The feature is inherently UI — an inspector over state the host already serves (`getPiHarnessRuntime`; `AgentPanel` renders one slice today; the 63 prepared i18n keys are its copy). The Phase-4 design gate still applies, but it decides the FORM only (extend `AgentPanel` vs a separate panel; omnigent surfaces reviewed for borrowable patterns), not whether. The delete-keys branch is dead. **SUPERSEDED 2026-09-01 (owner): DO NOT BUILD** — a Pi-only inspector manufactures the divergence this wave closes; P4.7 carries the ruling and the three recording items that remain.
- **DR-2 — background auto-commit: RESOLVED 2026-08-22 — split approved.** Commit half (M) lands here as P2.11; draft-MR half (L, GitLab forge integration) goes to a separate forge/git-UI plan together with the git panel and integrated terminal (Dev-4). Scope note: this applies to BACKGROUND SESSIONS (sessions finishing work unattended — backgrounded/agent-view sessions, spawned worktree children), not to background shell commands, and never to a session the user is actively driving.
- **DR-3 — codex vetoes: RESOLVED 2026-08-22 — no vetoes; Phase 3 proceeds as written.**
- **DR-4 — security plugins: RESOLVED 2026-08-22 — taken as a SUPPORTED INSTALL PATH, not bundled.** Owner's condition was "if it creates no problems"; bundling creates three (redistributing a third-party artifact, supply-chain quarantine into our release, staleness vs the marketplace), the install path creates none — our Claude format adapter was built against `claude-security` itself and the install is verified against the real artifact. Lands as P2.12 + P3.8; not-bundling recorded as Dev-16.

## Controller failure (2026-08-29): my own commit swept up a running lane's staged work

Pinning four rows, I ran `git add <plan>` then `git commit` with no pathspec — the
form this plan's own lane rules mandate, precisely because a pathspec commit takes
WORKING-TREE state. With ten lanes running, a sibling had `claude-agent.ts` and
`pi-agent.ts` staged mid-edit, and a no-pathspec commit commits the INDEX: my
docs-only commit carried 185 lines of someone else's unfinished work.

Recovered with `git reset --soft HEAD~1`, which restores the index exactly as it
was, then a pathspec commit of the plan alone; the sibling's two files were left
staged and untouched, so its own commit is unaffected.

**The rule inverts for the controller, and only for the controller.** A lane must
never use a pathspec, because it does not own its files exclusively and the
working tree moves under it. The controller is the SOLE writer of the tracker, so
for the plan file working-tree state and intent are identical, and the pathspec
form is the safe one — it is the only form that cannot pick up a neighbour's index.
Pin with `git commit <plan> -m …`, never `git add` + bare `git commit`.


**Same day, corrected twice more, and the rule above is only half right.** Two lanes
measured the other direction while it was still being broadcast:

- A lane's PATHSPEC commit swept a neighbour's 163 uncommitted lines out of
  `scripts/check-typecheck-coverage.ts` — because a pathspec commit takes
  WORKING-TREE state, and two lanes were editing that file.
- A lane's bare commit took a third lane's seven staged files, including its
  entire finished body of work, so three rows landed under another row's subject.

**So neither form is the fix, and choosing between them was the wrong question.**
A bare commit leaks through the shared INDEX; a pathspec commit leaks through the
shared WORKING TREE. Both are safe only when no other lane touches the file, and
the actual defect was mine: I asserted zones were disjoint from row titles without
verifying it. `pi-agent.ts` and `claude-agent.ts` were each held by two lanes at
once, and `scripts/check-typecheck-coverage.ts` by two more.

The rule that survives: **derive each lane's file set before dispatch, intersect
the sets, and sequence any lane whose intersection is non-empty** — the guide's own
"two units needing one file run in sequence", applied to a set I never computed.
Where a file genuinely must be shared, the working form is the one a lane invented
under pressure: build the index blob as HEAD plus only your own regions, then verify
hunk-by-hunk that no foreign hunk is staged. That is expensive, which is the point —
it is the cost of a zone that was not exclusive.


**Third and fourth confirmations, same day.** A lane building its fix inside
`splitCompoundCommand` needed an edit to `removal-circuit-breaker.test.ts`, and a
sibling lane writing that same file **silently clobbered it** — confirmed by hunk
headers, the surviving diff entirely the sibling's. It restructured so the file
needed no change at all, so nothing was lost; the next lane told that file is its
own will hit the same clobber. Separately, the window lane could not use the
pathspec form on `pi-agent.ts` and `claude-agent.ts` at all, because a sibling's
teardown work sat in the working tree, and had to build patches of only its own
hunks and `git apply --cached` them.

So three files were contested, not two, and the working form under contention is
the one two lanes independently arrived at: **stage only your own hunks against
HEAD, then verify `git diff --cached` lists nothing else before committing.**
That is the manual price of a zone I failed to compute.


**A fifth controller error, cheaper but the same shape (2026-08-29, wave 6).** Two
lane briefs cited `scripts/.lane-guard.sh` as "a working refusal harness in this
tree". **It does not exist.** I had seen it once in `git status` as an UNTRACKED
file a lane created mid-wave, and by the time I quoted it, it was gone. The lane
that went looking wrote its own (`scripts/gate-safety.ts`) and reported the miss.

The rule this earns is the same one AGENTS.md already applies to documentation
anchors, and I did not apply it to my own briefs: **verify a path exists before
citing it, and never cite an untracked file as a durable example** — an untracked
file is one lane's scratch, not a repository fact.


**A fifth contention shape, and a new banned verb (2026-08-29, wave 9).** A lane ran
`git commit --amend --no-edit -- <its own paths>` to fold in a precision fix. A sibling
had committed in the gap, so **the amend landed on the sibling's commit** — the tip had
moved under it. The lane detected this, restored the sibling's commit to its original
SHA with its original four files via `git reset --soft` plus targeted `git restore
--staged`, verified byte-for-byte, and landed its own fix as a separate commit. The
controller re-verified: `d3ea9ed03` still shows 4 files and 305 insertions, exactly as
its own lane reported.

**So the rule gains a verb: `--amend` is unsafe with lanes on one branch, for the same
reason `-a` and a bare `git commit` are** — all three read shared state at a moment the
author does not control. `--amend` is worse than the other two, because it rewrites a
commit somebody else has already reported a SHA for. A lane that wants a precision fix
lands a second commit.


**The instruction alone was not a mechanism (2026-08-29, wave 9).** Every brief in
this wave said the controller is the plan file's only writer. **Three of fifteen
lanes wrote to it anyway** — and they were not being careless: each had rows to pin,
each used a careful technique, and one of them repaired a sibling's commit
byte-for-byte afterwards. One pathspec commit of mine then swallowed two of their
rows into a message that does not mention them, and a lane's `--amend` raced mine.

Nothing was lost — verified: 781 rows, all seven cells, phase order clean, both
contested rows pinned with their real SHAs, and the sibling's 87 uncommitted lines
intact. But that is luck plus three careful lanes, not a property of the design.

**The failure is mine and it is structural: at fifteen lanes the plan file is a
contention point, and a rule that only I may write it is not enforceable by asking.**
Either the controller pins continuously enough that no lane ever has a reason to
reach for it, or lanes get a mechanism — a per-lane row file the controller folds
in, or an append-only side-channel. Repeating the instruction louder is the one
option measured not to work.


**A third commit form, and a new hazard it leaves behind (2026-08-29, wave 10).**
A lane needed to commit six files while BOTH locale files carried a sibling's
in-flight hunks (so a pathspec commit would sweep them) AND the shared index held
sibling-staged renderer deletions (so a bare commit would sweep those). Neither
approved form was safe. It built a **private index** — `GIT_INDEX_FILE=.git/index-<row>`
holding HEAD plus only its own hunks — verified the staged path list, and committed
from that.

**The hazard is what it leaves behind, and it is worse than the problem it solves.**
Afterwards the SHARED index still pointed those six files at the PRE-commit HEAD:
**a staged revert of the commit that had just landed.** The next lane to run a bare
`git commit` would have applied it, silently undoing work that was already in the
history and attributing the undo to nobody. The lane found it and reset those paths
to the new HEAD.

So the private-index form is legitimate under double contention, and **it is
incomplete without the reset**: after committing from a private index, `git reset --
<your paths>` against the shared one, and verify. Four commit forms are now on
record here — bare, pathspec, private-index, and `--amend` — and only the last is
banned outright; the other three are each safe in a case and unsafe in another.


**A contention shape that is not about committing at all (2026-08-29, wave 10).** A
lane wrote ten keys into a locale file; a sibling then performed a **full-file
write** of that same locale — a whole-object serialise-and-save, not a hunk — and
**silently erased them.** No conflict, no error, nothing in `git status` to suggest
a loss: the file simply no longer contained the earlier lane's work.

Every commit-form rule on record is about which SNAPSHOT a commit takes. This one
is upstream of that: **two writers, last-write-wins, and the loser cannot tell.**
The affected lane noticed only because it re-read its own file before committing,
then landed its keys surgically (HEAD plus its own ten lines) and restored the
sibling's in-flight edits afterwards.

The rule this earns: **for a file any lane may rewrite wholesale — the locales are
the known case — re-read your own contribution immediately before staging, and
treat a missing line as expected rather than impossible.** And a lane that
serialises a whole config or locale object should say so in its report, because the
loss it causes is invisible to everyone else.


**The sharpest statement of the hazard yet, from a lane that hit it and undid it
cleanly (2026-08-29, wave 11): verifying the index and then committing from it is
NOT ATOMIC on this box.** The lane ran `git diff --cached`, saw only its own paths,
and in the window before its `git commit` a sibling staged **six** files. The commit
swept them. It undid this with `git reset --soft HEAD~1`, **which restored their
staged state exactly**, unstaged only its own paths, and redid the commit from a
private index — afterwards verifying the shared index held exactly the sibling's six
files, byte-identical.

Every earlier note here treats the commit forms as a question of *which snapshot*.
This one names the real property: **the check and the commit are two operations, and
another process runs between them.** No amount of verifying makes a shared-index
commit safe while lanes are live; only a private index removes the window.

Also recorded, because it cost several minutes of red across unrelated lanes: a
lane briefly left `config-writer.ts` unparseable by writing prose containing `*/`
inside a block comment, which terminated the comment early. Every `bun test` that
imports the codex adapter failed until it was fixed. **A comment is code to the
parser** — the same class as the URL in a string literal that broke a scanner's
comment stripping earlier in this run.


**Controller correction to the acceptance rule itself (2026-08-30, wave 12).** Every
brief in this run has said *acceptance is mutant survival by exact reverse text
replacement, hash confirmed*. **The reverse-replacement half is the wrong primitive
and P2.452 measured why: a guard on the reverse side can only report corruption,
never prevent it.** With a uniqueness guard the restore refuses and the file stays
mutated; without one the restore reports success and leaves the file wrong in two
places in opposite directions, with nothing but the hash disagreeing. Three lanes
hit this in two waves and every one of them was saved by the hash check, not by the
swap.

**The rule from here: restore by writing the whole pre-mutation file back — or
`git show HEAD:<path>` each cycle — then assert the hash. A reverse swap is a last
resort, and if it is unavoidable, its anchor must be checked for presence AND
uniqueness BEFORE the forward write, not after.** The hash assertion stays
mandatory either way; it is the only thing that has actually caught this.

I will carry the corrected form into every brief from here. The lanes already
running were given the old wording, so their reports may describe a swap — that is
my instruction, not their shortcut.



**The shared scratchpad is NOT lane-private, and a text-mode mutator silently rewrites line endings (measured z-w12).** Two instrument failures from one lane, both of which produced a *successful-looking* wrong result:

- The scratchpad directory this run hands every lane is **one directory, 431 files deep**, and siblings **overwrote a lane's helper script mid-run**. A lane that writes `probe.py` and runs it two minutes later may be running someone else's probe. Lanes must use inline heredocs or a name carrying their own row id — and a controller must stop describing that directory as per-lane, which these briefs did.
- A text-mode mutation helper **rewrote every line ending** in a vendored `.d.ts` that ships CRLF. The forward mutation and the reverse replacement both reported success, the diff of the two anchor lines was exactly as intended, and **the file was wrong from its first byte to its last.** The only instrument that saw it was the restore hash.

**That is the THIRD independent confirmation of the corrected acceptance rule**, and the first from outside the mutation itself: a reverse text replacement can report success on a file it has corrupted globally. Restore by writing the whole pre-mutation file back, or by `git show HEAD:<path>`, and assert the hash — the hash is not a belt-and-braces check beside the swap, it is **the only load-bearing part of the pair.**


**Two instruments in one column: `grep -c` counts LINES and `grep -o | wc -l` counts MATCHES, and this tree recorded both as one number (measured z-w12).** A probe table in this plan mixed the two, so `allowedPluginMarketplaces 3` was lines while `org-provisioned 3` was occurrences. **Five of eight strings differ**, two of them by more than double.

The correction is not to pick one. **The ratio is itself the finding:** the vendored binary carries every user-visible string **twice** — once in a string table and once in embedded JS — so a line count and a match count diverge systematically, and a claim of the form *"appears N times"* means nothing without saying which instrument produced N. Keep both columns.

**Every recorded binary-probe count in this plan predating this correction is therefore of unknown units** unless the row says which command produced it. Two consequences: a `ᵏ` marker is weaker evidence than it looks, and the reader-shape probe P2.442 built (the name followed by `:` or `=`, against a live sibling control) is the form to copy — it answers *is this read* rather than *does this appear*, which is the question a guard actually turns on.

Also noted: a lane recorded a flaky suite at **load average 28.97 with a background `git gc` running**. That is the load confound this plan already ruled on — a timing or flake claim needs the load quoted beside it, and this one correctly was.

**And one lane caught itself deriving a doc anchor instead of reading it**, then fixed it by byte offset and **recorded the slip in the row rather than silently correcting it**. That is the behaviour the anchor rule is for: the rule exists because derived slugs have been wrong in both directions, and a lane that reports its own near-miss is worth more than one that quietly gets it right.


**A commit that is actually atomic, built by a lane rather than prescribed by me (measured z-w12) — and it is strictly better than the pathspec form these briefs mandate.**

The standing rule has been *commit with an explicit pathspec, because a bare commit takes a sibling's work*. That rule is correct and **still insufficient**: `git commit <pathspec>` takes each named file's **working-tree** state, so it is safe only if nobody else has touched those exact paths, and *checking* that is not atomic with *committing* it.

The lane that shared `SessionManager.ts` with another session's uncommitted work never ran `git commit` at all:

1. reconstruct the intended content from `git show HEAD:<path>` plus its own edits, in a scratch file;
2. `diff` that against the working tree and confirm the **only** difference is the other session's known hunks;
3. stage the blobs into a **private `GIT_INDEX_FILE`**, so the shared index is never touched;
4. `write-tree` / `commit-tree`, then move the branch with a **compare-and-swap** `update-ref <new> <old>`;
5. `git reset -- <its own paths>` afterwards.

**HEAD moved twice mid-flight** — siblings committed while it worked — and the CAS caught it both times; a re-derivation came out byte-identical. Step 5 was not hygiene: the shared index **held a staged revert of the lane's own commit**, 657 deletions, which a later sibling's pathspec commit could have landed.

Two consequences. First, this is the protocol for **any lane sharing a file with uncommitted work it does not own** — the pathspec form stays the default for exclusive files, because it is far cheaper. Second, and more general: **the failure mode I have been guarding against is not *the wrong files get committed*, it is *the index is a shared mutable global*.** A private index removes the shared object; a CAS removes the check-then-act. Everything else is mitigation.


**A green measurement can contain a DEAD ARM, and two rows in this plan concluded from one (measured z-w13).** Two predecessor rows recorded that a runtime *accepts* a bare IPv6 `no_proxy` entry. It does not. The reason they concluded otherwise: **every arm of both measurements used a `127.0.0.1` URL**, so the `127.0.0.1` entry in the same list did the bypassing and the IPv6 entry under test **was never exercised**. The runs were green, the controls were real, and the conclusion was still wrong.

This is the positive-control rule's blind spot. A control proves the *instrument* works; it does not prove the instrument **reached the thing under test**. The form that catches it is a **discriminating** arm — one that must fail if the subject is inert — and the lane that found this built one: the entry alone, with no sibling that could satisfy the match.

The same lane found the same shape in a test: a pre-existing IPv6 case passed **with an empty rule array**, riding an unconditional exemption, so it could never have failed on the parser it claimed to cover. **Both instances were invisible to every gate and to review.** The question to ask of any passing arm is not *did it pass* but **what would have to break for this to fail** — and if the answer is *nothing in the subject*, it is a dead arm regardless of its colour.

Also recorded, as a technique worth copying: that lane proved typecheck **reach** into each changed file by **planting a deliberate type error and reverting it**, rather than trusting a green run. Given that `typecheck:all` is an `&&` chain that stops at the first red, a planted error is currently the only direct proof a specific file was reached.


**I asserted a convention that does not exist, for the second time this run (z-w13).** A brief told a lane to *follow the existing `ensureTool` convention in that file* — there is **no `ensureTool` in this repo at all**; the single occurrence is a comment about a dependency's own helper. The lane recorded the null instead of inventing around it, which is the correct behaviour and the reason no damage was done.

This is the same defect as citing `scripts/.lane-guard.sh` as *a working example in this tree* when it did not exist. Both times the invented detail was **plausible, specific, and load-bearing for how the lane was told to work**. The rule for briefs, now twice-earned: **verify that a named file, symbol, or convention exists before instructing a lane to follow it** — a brief is not a place to reason from what a codebase *should* have.

**And I misdiagnosed a live diagnostic in two directions at once.** I flagged four `TS80007` warnings to a lane with two readings — stale awaits, or a signature that should be async — and told it one of them must hold. Neither did: the awaits are six weeks old, and the inaccurate declaration is a **dependency's**, not ours. **Offering a lane a closed set of explanations is itself a way of being wrong**, because it forecloses the answer that the premise is misattributed. The lane's own framing is the one to copy: it measured what the expression returns before choosing between remedies, and then declined to fix it inside an unrelated commit.


**I scoped a zone too narrow to satisfy the requirement I wrote into the same row (z-w13).** P2.463's row said *four things must move together or the tree lies*, and I then listed a zone containing three of them. The fourth sits in a different package path. The lane did the right thing — completed three, dispatched the fourth, and **stated plainly that the row's own one-commit requirement was unsatisfiable as scoped** — but the tree spent that interval describing a state it was not in, which is the exact defect the row existed to prevent.

The controller lesson is narrow and mechanical: **when a row's correctness argument is *these must land together*, the zone must be computed from the list, not written beside it.** I derived the zone from the files I had seen in the predecessor's report rather than from the row's own four clauses. Two of the seven docblocks that actually fell were **invisible to a search for the subject**, because they carried a *count* of affected entries instead of naming any — so even a diligent zone computed by grep would have missed them, and the only instrument that finds that shape is reading the module header.

Same run, same class as inventing an `ensureTool` convention and citing a file that did not exist: **all three are the controller describing the codebase from memory instead of measuring it.**


**The editor's diagnostics and the repo's gate are different instruments, and I escalated two of them as if they were the same (measured z-w13).** `noUnusedLocals` and `noUnusedParameters` are `false` in all three tsconfigs, so **`TS6133` is invisible to `typecheck:all` by design.** Every unused-identifier hint I forwarded to a lane this wave came from an option set the gate does not use — which means it could not have regressed anything, and **no gate will ever report it either.**

Both escalations were also wrong about causation. The first I offered as *stale awaits or a signature that should be async*; the answer was a dependency's declaration. The second I offered as *inert waiver, load-bearing waiver, or one of four missed shapes*; the answer was that the file **carries no directive at HEAD at all**, so the row I asked about could not have touched it, and the two identifiers were dead before the run began.

Three rules, all cheap, all earned:
- **Before forwarding a diagnostic, check whether the repo's own gate can see it.** If it cannot, it is an observation for a row, not an interruption for a lane.
- **Establish ownership from `git show HEAD:<path>` before naming a suspect.** One command settled what two rounds of inference did not.
- **Do not hand a lane a closed set of explanations.** Twice now the true answer was outside the set, and a list of candidates reads as a constraint on where to look.


**I inverted a row's premise while paraphrasing it into a brief (z-w13), and it is the fourth of this exact kind.** The row said a capability was vacuous **off Pi**. My brief rendered that as *there is no workflow surface on Pi at all* — the inverse. The predecessor commit had **added** a support table in which **Pi is the only runtime that has the surface**.

The lane caught it because the brief also told it to read that commit before writing the verdict, and it did. That instruction is the only reason the inversion cost nothing, which makes it the generalisable part: **a brief that paraphrases a row must also name the primary source the lane can check the paraphrase against.**

Four errors this run, one family: an invented `ensureTool` convention, a cited file that did not exist, a zone narrower than the row's own four-clause requirement, and now a paraphrase that reversed the subject. **All four are the controller writing from memory where a one-command check was available**, and in three of the four the lane's own discipline absorbed the error. That is not a safety margin to spend — it is three near misses.

The concrete rule, now applied: **quote the row's sentence into the brief verbatim rather than restating it**, and let the restatement live only in the surrounding explanation where a lane can see both.


**"Rendered by nothing" is not "read by nothing", and the reader nobody counts is the LIVE-TEST RIG (measured z-w13).** A row asserted that a runtime security block was *computed, wired and rendered by nothing*, and proposed deletion. True of rendered. One of its fields is read by the CDP live-case driver, whose own comment says it is *the only read that separates a card already answered from a second, genuinely pending request* — so deleting the block would have **blinded a live case while every unit gate stayed green**.

This is the guide's own *a live case's DETECTOR is the thing most likely to be wrong* rule arriving from the other side: not a detector that reports falsely, but a detector **deleted as dead code** by a sweep that never looked in `scripts/`.

Two rules, both cheap:
- **Any dead-surface claim must enumerate readers in four places, not one:** production code, contract tests, the live-test rig under `scripts/cdp/`, and the built bundle. P2.364 checked all four and the last one changed the row's cost argument entirely — the keys were not merely parity-checked, they were **shipped to every user**.
- **Split *display-dead* from *data-dead* before deleting.** The keys were dead; the data behind them was not. A row that conflates the two produces a diff that looks like cleanup and lands as a capability loss.

Also recorded: the archaeology this row required was **impossible on-branch**, because history stops at a squashed 880-file import. `git log --all -S<string>` found the introducing and deleting commits in one command. **Where a plan row says *find what was meant to consume this*, `--all` is not optional.**


**Killing a lane mid-cycle leaves a LIVE MUTANT in the working tree (measured z-w13, and it was my kill).** The wave was paused under time pressure and the last lane was stopped between a mutant's forward write and its restore. Its final line was *M9 killed. One more to isolate the clause assertion itself* — so the file on disk carried a hard-coded string where the source should have named a constant, **and it looked like ordinary in-progress work.** The only thing that made it legible was reading the diff before deciding what to do with the file.

This is the corrupted-baseline hazard this plan has documented three times, arriving from a direction none of those three anticipated: **not a failed restore, but a restore that never got to run.**

The recovery protocol, now standing:
1. **Read the diff of every file a killed lane left dirty**, before touching it. A live mutant is indistinguishable from a draft at the file level.
2. **Preserve the draft to a path whose NAME carries the warning**, then restore from `git show HEAD:<path>` and assert the hash. Nothing is lost and nothing is trusted.
3. **Record the draft as a design record, not a patch** — the reasoning is the expensive part and it survives; the diff must be re-derived.

And the asymmetric lesson: **a lane's commit body can be a complete report.** The lane never sent one, yet its commit carried the measurement, the refused alternative, the per-runtime verdict and the full mutant table with hash chains. That row was pinned with no loss. **Where a report is a courtesy, the commit message is the artifact** — a brief should say so.


**A `**` pathspec handed to `git grep` is read WITHOUT glob magic and silently drops files (measured z-w14).** A lane counting occurrences with `packages/shared/src/**/*.ts` got **24 hits over 14 files** and missed one file entirely; with `:(glob)packages/shared/src/**/*.ts` it got exactly **25**. No error, no warning — just a smaller number that looks like an answer.

This is the third distinct way an absence or a count has been wrong in this plan, and they fail differently, so all three checks are needed:
- **NUL bytes** — plain `grep` skips the file silently; use `grep -a`.
- **Case** — a lower-case pattern misses every sentence-opening occurrence; a case-sensitive grep over prose is not an absence claim.
- **Pathspec globbing** — `git` reads `**` literally unless you write `:(glob)`, so the file set is quietly narrower than you asked for.

**And the deeper version of the same lesson, now measured twice in one family: a grep is not a rule run.** P2.229 recorded 40 where the rule gave 172; P2.477's row recorded 25 call sites where the rule gave 16, because nine of them sat **inside string literals** that no linter reads as code. Where a tool can answer the question itself — `eslint --print-config`, a throwaway tsconfig, the rule enabled in a scratch config — **run the tool.** A grep answers *does this text appear*; the question is almost always *does this apply*.


**I accused a lane of another lane's file, from the same inference I had recorded as an error two waves earlier (z-w14).** A parse error appeared in `managed-marketplace-entries.ts`; the file was `M` in the tree and different at HEAD, so I told the proxy lane it was theirs. It was not. `git diff` on that file showed **+238/−11 of a marketplace lane's work** — obviously not a proxy change, and one command away.

The reasoning I used, *modified in the tree and different at HEAD therefore yours*, **does not hold on a box with roughly thirty concurrently modified files.** It is the same shape as the four errors already recorded here: an invented convention, a cited file that never existed, a zone narrower than its own row's requirement, and a paraphrase that reversed a row. **Fifth of one family, and the fifth time a lane's own discipline absorbed it.**

The operative rule, now stated as a command rather than a principle: **`git diff -- <file> | head` before naming an owner.** Content identifies a lane; status does not.

**The defect itself is a trap worth keeping.** The docblock was quoting a documentation example of a glob — `*/plugins` — and **`*/` inside a block comment closes the comment early**, leaving stray tokens the parser reads as a module declaration. Nine hard errors from one quoted example. The owning lane's fix is the right shape: write the examples out in words, with a note saying that a star followed by a slash closes a block comment. **Any docblock quoting a glob, a regex or a path pattern has to be checked for that sequence** — and this plan's own rule to *quote the verbatim sentence* makes the collision more likely, not less.


**ONE SYNTAX ERROR IN ONE FILE MAKES `tsc` BLIND TO EVERY SEMANTIC ERROR IN THE REPO (measured z-w14, and it invalidates evidence).** A sibling's uncommitted block-comment defect produced three syntax errors, and `tsc` **reports the syntactic category instead of the semantic one**: `typecheck:electron` and `typecheck:shared` both exited 2 naming only that file — and were blind to everything else. **Proven, not inferred: a deliberate `const x: number = "s"` planted in another module was NOT reported.**

So every `typecheck:*` run taken while that file was broken is **worthless as evidence of anything but that file**, and several lanes ran one in that window. The exit code was non-zero, so nothing looked green — **the failure mode is not a false pass, it is a true failure that HIDES all the others**, which is worse, because a lane reading *one error, not mine, in a sibling's file* correctly concludes it is unaffected and incorrectly concludes its own code was checked.

Two rules follow, and the first is cheap:
- **A `typecheck` failure naming only files outside your change proves nothing about your change.** Re-run in an isolated worktree, or plant a deliberate type error in your own file and confirm it is reported — the same positive-control discipline this plan already demands of absence claims, applied to a gate.
- **This is the third instrument that reports success or a narrow failure while telling you nothing** — beside the `&&` chain that skipped nine packages, and the pipefail trap where `$?` after a pipe read 0 while the compiler exited 2. All three are *gates that stop gating quietly*.

**And a lane reported its own corruption rather than burying it.** It mutated **before taking the test mutex**, so its mutant sat in the tree while a sibling ran a suite; then `kill -9` bypassed the shell's EXIT trap and **left the mutant on disk**. Every verdict taken after that was measured against corrupted source and was **discarded rather than reconciled** — which is the correct response and the harder one. Its rerun holds one lock across mutate/test/restore and re-checks `git diff --quiet` after every mutant. It also wrote down that a sibling seeing an unexplained failure in a named ten-minute window may have been seeing its mutant. **That sentence is worth more than the fix: on a shared tree, a lane's mutation is everyone's flake, and the mutex is not an optimisation.**


**I checked a killed lane's dirty files against MY list of its zone, and my list was three of twenty (z-w14).** After stopping a lane I reported its footprint as three files. It had twenty, and the seventeen I did not see were intact — so no harm followed, but the method was wrong in the direction that matters: **a filtered `git status -- <paths>` can only ever show files I already knew about**, and the whole point of inspecting a killed lane is to find what I did not know. Use unfiltered `git status --porcelain` and let the lane's report tell me which are its; never the reverse.

**And I asserted when it died from its last transcript line.** I read *"Now mutation-proof the two findings I actually closed"* and concluded it had been killed at the start of the mutation cycle. It had been killed **after the cycle completed**, and what was running was an optional low-load control — which returned, and changed a claim. **The last line of a transcript is where the model announced an intention, not where it stopped.**

Both are the same family as the four already recorded: a conclusion reached from something adjacent to the evidence rather than the evidence. Sixth and seventh instances. **The lanes have absorbed every one of them, which is not a margin to keep spending.**

**Two new traps from the same lane, both worth more than the row:**
- **Naming a dead anchor in prose CITES it.** The doc-anchor guard reported a dead anchor from inside the sentence explaining that it is dead, and the row's own `page.md` › `#section` — written to name the defect *shape* — scored as a real citation. Split every specimen across two code spans. This tree's own habit of quoting exact tokens makes the collision certain, not unlikely.
- **A one-line `grep -c` is not an absence test for a verbatim SENTENCE**, because the sentence may be **line-wrapped in the source**. Two of four scored zero and were live; the one that happened to fit on a line was the positive control that prevented two phantom quotes being filed. Match on a distinctive fragment, or strip newlines before searching.


**Commits land that no tracker row claims — the mirror of the citation defect, and the more dangerous direction (measured z-w15).** A lane found **two of its four rows already closed at HEAD**, by commits appearing in **zero** tracker rows. So alongside *a row citing a commit not on this branch*, the tree also holds *commits no row cites* — and this direction is worse, because the first misleads an auditor while the second **sends a lane to redo finished work.**

Both are cheap to detect and neither was being checked:
- **Every SHA a row cites must resolve AND be an ancestor of HEAD.** 185 of 185 resolved; 2 were off-branch.
- **Every commit on the branch should be claimed by some row**, or be deliberately unclaimed (a controller commit, a merge, a revert). An unclaimed feature commit is either an unpinned row or work nobody planned.

The second check is the one that would have saved this lane its re-verification. It is not free — 1296 commits against 853 rows — but it is a one-off script, and the finding it produces is exactly the *does it add up* question the owner asked.


**The foreign-hunk count I gave a lane was READING-DEPENDENT, and I stated it as a fact (z-w15).** I told one lane the shared session file carried *three* foreign hunks and a later lane *four*. Measured: `git diff | grep -c '^@@'` gives **2** and `git diff -U0 | grep -c '^@@'` gives **3** — the same two edits, counted by two instruments. A lane checking against my number would have concluded the tree had changed under it when nothing had.

The rule that follows is small and general: **when a brief hands a lane a count, it must hand the command too.** Not because the number ages — that is already recorded — but because a count with no instrument is unfalsifiable, and the lane's only options are to trust it or to re-derive it silently.

**Also recorded, so nobody re-attributes it:** the other session's uncommitted work in that file causes **7 of the 10 failures** in its test directory. Established by a two-arm control — the same seven fail with a lane's change applied and with it reverted — not by assumption. Three more pass in isolation and are cross-file interference. Any lane touching that directory should expect those ten and own none of them.


**I put a NON-EXISTENT FILE PATH in a lane's zone, for the second time this run (z-w15).** A brief named `packages/shared/src/config/permissions-config.ts`; the file is `packages/shared/src/agent/permissions-config.ts`. The same brief named a service file as a surface of the row — it is not one, and a lane proved it by reading: that file searches only session transcripts, has one caller, and **filtering there would BE the failure the row warns against**, by construction. A third claim, that a second executor was a live construction site, was also false — it is constructed only in tests.

Three false claims in one zone block. The first cost a sibling nothing because that lane read before it wrote; the second and third would have sent a lane to build in the wrong place.

**Ninth instance of one family this run**, and the family is now precisely nameable: **every one is the controller asserting a fact about the codebase that a single command would have settled.** An invented convention, a cited file that never existed, a zone narrower than its own row's requirement, a reversed paraphrase, a filtered status check, a transcript line read as a stopping point, an owner named from a file's status, a reading-dependent count, and now two wrong paths and a wrong surface.

The mechanical rule, which is the only kind that has held: **every path in a zone block gets `ls` or `git ls-files` before the brief is sent.** It is one command for six lanes and it would have caught all four path errors.


**Two more of the same family, and then the rule caught the rest (z-w15).** I sent a lane a correction meant for a **different lane that has not been dispatched yet** — it belongs to echelon 2 and I addressed echelon 1's roster. The lane read it, saw it named files outside its pinned zone, and **correctly declined to act**, which is the only reason it cost nothing.

Then I applied the mechanical rule from the previous entry — `ls` every path in every brief before sending — **and it found two more non-existent paths in the undispatched briefs**, in two different lanes. Both are now corrected against `find`. All 43 distinct paths across all fifteen briefs are verified present.

**The rule works and the judgement did not.** Nine instances were needed before the check existed; the check found the tenth and eleventh in one command. Anything a brief asserts about the tree — a path, a count, a convention, a symbol — belongs to that same class.

**And an independent confirmation of P2.231 arrived from a lane that had not read it:** its disposable worktree was **not isolated**, because symlinking the dependency directory wholesale made the relative workspace links resolve back into the **main** tree — so the worktree ran a sibling's in-flight file and reported an error from code it was never meant to see. That is P2.231's exact mechanism, found again, by a lane escaping sibling churn and getting the opposite. **Two independent measurements of one trap in one wave is the strongest evidence this plan has for a rig defect.**


**I told a lane the owner's pause list held four rows. It holds five (z-w15).** The fifth is `P4.10`, and I had measured that myself two hours earlier when I listed the paused rows — then wrote *four* into a brief from memory. The lane checked the section text, found five, and said so in its first paragraph.

Twelfth instance, same family, and it closes the argument the previous entries were building: **the mechanical check now exists for paths and it works, and this one was a count — a different shape of the same assertion.** So the rule generalises: **anything a brief states about the tree — a path, a count, a list, a convention — is quoted from a command's output or it is not stated.** Not *checked before sending*; **quoted**, so the lane can see the instrument and re-run it.


**Two environment traps from one lane, both of which produce a confident wrong answer (z-w15).**

**In zsh, a loop variable named `path` clobbers `PATH`.** A lane running the private-index commit protocol had `git` vanish mid-sequence for that reason. No partial commit was produced, but the failure reads as a broken protocol rather than a shell quirk. Rename the variable; never iterate into `path`.

**And the shared-dependency symlink produced a RED TYPECHECK for a healthy file** — the same trap P2.231 documents, in its third independent sighting this wave. The lane's own words are the rule: *recording it as a finding would have sent someone to audit a healthy file.* It confirmed against the real tree before reporting. **A red gate observed only inside an unisolated worktree is not evidence about the code.**

**And the controller fixed a red the fleet inherited, for the second time this wave.** `typecheck:ui` was failing at HEAD for every lane — a readonly tuple handed to a table-driven test, from a commit that landed hours earlier — found not by the lane that caused it but by a gate lane running the full typecheck and **attributing the red to the commit that caused it rather than to its own work.** That attribution discipline is what made it actionable; the fix was two characters at each of two call sites.


**The atomic commit protocol needs one more refusal: a written tree identical to the base (measured z-w15).** A lane's first attempt produced an **empty commit that moved the ref** — zsh does not word-split an unquoted variable, so `git update-index` received one giant path, errored, and `set -e` did not stop the script, **which then committed HEAD's own tree under the lane's message.** It was caught, the ref was CAS'd back, and the work re-committed from a bash array.

**The failure is silent and the artefact is worse than nothing: a commit whose message describes changes it does not contain.** Every later reader — a bisect, an audit resolving cited SHAs, a lane reading `git log` for the voice — is misled by a commit that looks completed.

Two additions to the protocol, both cheap:
- **Build the pathspec list as a bash array**, never an unquoted variable — zsh's word-splitting differs from bash's and this tree's lanes run under zsh.
- **Refuse to commit when the written tree equals the base tree.** One comparison, and it is the only check that catches this class regardless of which shell quirk produced it.

This is the second zsh-specific trap this wave, after a loop variable named `path` clobbering `PATH` and making `git` vanish. **Neither is a git problem and both present as one.**


**The starved-run rule I put in every brief has a SECOND cause, and it is the more common one here (measured z-w15).** I have been teaching lanes that a suite dying with a timeout and **zero assertion failures** is starvation. That signature is real — and a lane measured a suite showing it that was **not starved at all**: a single module import in one hook costs **44.7 seconds** against a five-second default, a 9× overrun, while the hook's other three steps take 52 ms, 0 and 0.

**It presents as contention because the budget is a timer.** A one-second heartbeat beside that import ticked 13 times in 44.7 seconds with one **31.5-second gap**, so whether the run goes red is decided by where a yield lands — which is exactly what load-sensitivity looks like from outside.

**The control that separates them, and it is cheap:** run the same batch at both extremes. This lane's identical four-suite batch took **1.66 s at load 9.4** and **81.64 s at load 41→118** — a 49× spread — and passed **131 of 131 both times.** Load moves the duration; it did not move the verdict.

So the rule becomes two-sided:
- **Timeout + zero assertion failures + passes at low load** → starvation, register it as such.
- **Timeout + zero assertion failures + fails alone at low load too** → a genuinely slow step. **Profile the hook before attributing it**, and fix it with an explicit budget set against the **measured floor**, never zero.

**And a misnomer worth knowing: the runner prints the same *beforeEach/afterEach* message for the `beforeAll`/`afterAll` family**, so a row can name the wrong hook family in good faith from the output alone — this one did, and the lane's first probe carried both kinds and would have proved nothing either way.


**A brief's blanket phrasing nearly caused the deletion of a load-bearing widening (z-w16).** I wrote that a sibling's type fix *removed the workaround*, and a lane found a **fourth** site the row did not name whose comment made the same claim — **where only the reason was stale.** The fix changed the result type; the input type still carries neither field, so the widening there is still doing work. The lane established that by **reading the predecessor's diff rather than my summary**, and said so.

The rule this yields is narrow and worth keeping: **a brief may say *this specific claim is now false*; it may not say *this class of claim is now false*.** The second reads as permission to delete every instance, and the instances differ.

**And an instrument trap that touches every lane in this run: `bun test` given five paths RAN FOUR and said nothing about the missing one.** The lane caught it by reading the **file count** rather than the pass count — a green run over four of five suites is indistinguishable from a green run over five. Any lane naming explicit test paths should assert the file count it expected, and any *N pass / 0 fail* in a report is only as strong as the number of files behind it.


**A hazard in the atomic commit protocol itself, self-reported by the lane that hit it (z-w16): `git reset --` run while `GIT_INDEX_FILE` is still exported hits the PRIVATE index and leaves stale entries in the real one.** The protocol's final step exists precisely to clean the shared index, and with the variable still set it does the opposite — quietly, since the command succeeds. The lane caught it, re-ran with the variable unset, and verified nothing was staged and no sibling's dirty file had moved.

**Add to the protocol: unset `GIT_INDEX_FILE` before the reset, and verify the shared index is empty afterwards rather than assuming the reset did it.** That is the fourth refinement this protocol has taken from a lane that used it — after the compare-and-swap, the bash-array pathspec, and the refusal of a tree identical to the base. **Each one was found by a lane hitting it, none by design**, which is the argument for lanes reporting their own slips rather than quietly fixing them.


**An `Edit` that reports success on a contended file is NOT evidence the edit is on disk (measured z-w16).** A lane made two edits to a file a sibling was rewriting; **both were silently clobbered**, the tool reported success both times, and the lane found out only by re-grepping. Nothing failed, nothing warned.

This is the same shape as the empty commit that moved the ref: **an operation that succeeds while achieving nothing, leaving a report that says otherwise.** It is now the third member of that family in two waves, after the tree-identical commit and the reset that cleaned the wrong index.

The rule is one line and costs nothing: **after editing any file another lane may hold, re-read the changed region and confirm your text is there.** And the deeper rule the three of them share — **a success message from a tool is not a measurement; the file, the tree and the ref are.**

**The cross-lane coordination itself worked and is worth keeping as a pattern.** Rather than editing a sibling's file myself or letting the blocked lane route around it, I asked the holder to add three keywords and told the waiter to wait, naming the two workarounds it must not take. The export landed before the waiter committed, **it took no workaround, and it fed back two measurements I would not have had** — that the barrel needed no edit at all because it already re-exports the module, and that the import costs **zero milliseconds** because the module was already in the graph.


**A test that MIRRORS a rule tests the mirror (measured z-w16).** A lane's first suite restated the refusal rule instead of importing it, and its inversion mutant **survived every behavioural assertion** — because those assertions exercised the copy, which the mutant did not touch. **Only a source-level pin caught it.** The suite now drives the real export.

This is the sharpest form of a family this plan keeps meeting: the harness that throws the string it then asserts, the near-miss test whose set was empty, the fixture whose name was false. **All four are tests that cannot fail for the reason they claim.** The general check is cheap and worth making a habit: **mutate the production symbol and confirm the test reddens — if it does not, the test is reading something else.**

**And the same lane refuted its own stated reason with a control run.** It attributed a slow hook to a page import, then measured the suite running the same duration with itself absent, with a pre-existing pair accounting for the time. **The extraction it had done was still correct; the reason written in its header was not** — and it **left the wrong attribution in place, labelled**, rather than quietly deleting it. That is the right call: a corrected record teaches the next reader what the wrong inference looked like, and a deleted one teaches nothing.

## Controller failure (2026-08-25): the NUL control I handed every lane was itself dead
**And I walked into it in the commit that documented it — three times (z-w14).** The entry above records that *naming a dead anchor in prose CITES it*, and the pin note, the controller entry and a rider I wrote in that same commit each contained a bare `page.md` › `#section` or a bare codex anchor. The guard scored three new findings against the text explaining the trap.

That is not carelessness so much as the measure of how reliable the trap is: **the only way to write about a citation defect is to write the citation.** So the rule is mechanical, not a matter of care — **split every anchor token across two code spans on the way in, in prose as well as in code**, including the sentence saying why. And one consequence for the controller specifically: **run the guard after editing the tracker, not only after a lane edits source.** I have been treating that file as prose and it is scanned like everything else.


Measured on this rig, after a lane reported it:

- `grep -rlaP '\x00' --include='*.ts' packages/` → **`grep: invalid option -- P`**. This is
  BSD grep (`2.6.0-FreeBSD`); there is no `-P`. Piped through `wc -l` it prints **`0`**, which
  reads exactly like "no NUL-carrying files". **I put that command in brief after brief as
  "the correct control".** It is the same defect class this plan has been closing all week: an
  absence check that returns nothing for everything, and therefore cannot fail.
- **`rg` is not installed either** (`rg: command not found`), so every instruction of mine that
  said `rg -a`/`rg --pcre2` was unavailable. Lanes fell back to `grep -a`, which `AGENTS.md`
  actually prescribes, so that half cost nothing but noise.
- `AGENTS.md` never named the `-P` form. It says only: *"Some source files carry a NUL byte and
  plain grep skips them SILENTLY: use `grep -a` for any absence claim."* The broken command was
  mine, not the repo's.

**The control that works here**, and the one to use from now on:

```
python3 -c "
import os
n=0
for r,d,f in os.walk('packages'):
    if 'node_modules' in r: continue
    for x in f:
        if x.endswith(('.ts','.tsx')) and b'\x00' in open(os.path.join(r,x),'rb').read(): n+=1
print(n)"
```

→ **13**, and the list matches the one `AGENTS.md` implies: `marketplace/registry-source.ts`,
`marketplace/service.ts`, `agent/base-agent.ts`, `agent/permissions-config.ts`,
`agent/core/guardian-consult.ts`, `agent/memory/rule-matching.ts`, `sessions/mirror/in-memory.ts`,
`sessions/mirror/host.ts`, `telemetry/usage-metrics.ts`, `server-core/bootstrap/storage-runtime.ts`,
`server-core/projects/project-capability-watcher.ts`,
`server-core/sessions/__tests__/workspace-project-contract-corpus.test.ts`,
`server-core/handlers/rpc/capabilities.ts`.

**What I cannot tell from the reports, and will not pretend to:** several lanes wrote "NUL control
= 13 files". Thirteen is also the number written in `AGENTS.md`. So for those lanes I cannot
distinguish a measurement from a quotation, and any absence claim of theirs that rested on that
control should be treated as unverified until re-run with the command above. The lane that caught
this (`7df6f5788`) re-ran its own load-bearing enumeration with a byte scan for exactly that reason.


## Owner ruling 2026-09-10: the finish line — critical first, the rest to a follow-up plan, every open question by the balance rule, all three runtimes lifted, then the sitting and the release

Owner, in chat, six points, taken verbatim as the closing protocol of this plan:

1. **Finish everything critical** — every open row without which a user cannot work normally with the runtimes.
2. **The non-essential is deferred to the very end, and probably to a separate plan** — with a clear pass over what is left, so the owner can read what each remaining row is for.
3. **Every open question is answered NOW by the balance rule**: the recommendation that is closest to the runtimes' own documentation, with the least code, and with the simplest host coverage. No question waits for a sitting.
4. **All three runtimes are lifted to the latest versions available to us** — in Artifactory, and consistent with wherever CI takes them for a build.
5. **1–4 finished per plan, the CDP cases driven, a release made.**
6. **A follow-up plan is drafted** for what is left: the new integrations to update, and the authorization work.

### Where the runtimes come from, and what "latest available" reads as (measured 2026-09-10 against `bunfig.toml`'s registry, `.../api/npm/npm-all/`)

| Runtime | Shipped | Latest in Artifactory | Channel CI builds from | Lift target |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Agent SDK (`@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk` + the platform binary packages) | `0.3.233` (bundle self-report `2.1.233`) | `0.3.247` | the registry, `bun install --frozen-lockfile` | **`0.3.247`** |
| Pi (`@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent`, `pi-ai`, `pi-agent-core`) | `0.84.2` | `0.84.3` | the registry | **`0.84.3`** |
| codex (`codex-app-server` from the `openai/codex` GitHub release, tag in `packages/codex-protocol/manifest.json`; the Windows sandbox trio from npm `@openai/codex`) | `rust-v0.148.0` | npm `0.150.1` stable (`0.151.0` only as alphas; upstream `rust-v0.152.1` is NOT in the mirror) | the release asset for the app-server, the registry for the trio — one tag for both | **`rust-v0.150.1`** — the newest tag BOTH channels carry; P3.283's `0.152.1` would leave the Windows trio unreachable from Artifactory |

P3.283 is therefore answered: lift, to `rust-v0.150.1`, at the quiet-tree boundary. The 2026-08-29 directive stands in full for all three (*the difference covered or removed*, native-first) — a lift lane reads the upstream changelog between the two versions and reconciles every host mechanism the newer bundle now provides natively, and every behaviour that moves is a finding, not noise. Sequencing is unchanged: **no other lane in flight** while a lift runs, one runtime per lane, SDK → codex → Pi.

### The release sitting: the measure rows that gate 1.36.0, and the ones that do not

A `measure:` row is a live drive on the packaged build with the owner's credentials — it is not lane work. The ones without which a user's ordinary day on a runtime is unproven gate the release: **P3.352 P6.66 P6.91 P6.93 P6.107 P6.144 P6.150 P6.181 P6.187 P6.188 P6.194 P6.196 P6.198 P6.218 P6.226 P6.230 P6.265 P6.281 P6.282 P6.284 P6.287 P6.304 P6.408 P6.481 P6.544 P6.552 P6.854**, plus the two the W10 builds add (claude's native `EnterWorktree` through the floor, claude's `/rewind` restore). Every other `measure:` row — mostly second-order arms (managed clamps, prompt-cache switches, telemetry headers, hook output fields, plugin-scope corners) — carries `Deferred 2026-09-10 → follow-up plan` in its note and moves there with its verdicts intact when P7.7 drafts it.

### The follow-up plan's scope, as ruled

The deferred rows by id (each note names it), the two integration updates the lifts will surface as new upstream surfaces, and the authorization work (P6.538's identity arm is its first row). Drafted as P7.7 at close-out; nothing is moved out of this plan before that draft exists in the tree.


## Global Constraints

- Bun; `typecheck:all` never covers `packages/pi-agent-server` tests — tsc touched test files there via a config without the exclusion.
- Implementation-first verification budget (AGENTS.md) applies; permission/auth-surface diffs trigger the expanded final wave.
- i18n: any new renderer string lands in ALL locales; `lint:i18n:parity` + `lint:i18n:sorted` green.
- New UI states get playground `ComponentEntry` rows (module spread into `componentRegistry` AND its `Category` present in `categoryOrder`, or it vanishes silently).
- Probes exclude `apps/electron/resources/*` bundles and `codex-protocol/{schema,generated}`; `rg -a`/`grep -a` for absence claims, always with a positive control.
- Branch `feat/TCODE-000`; one commit per task with the row's subject; no Co-Authored-By trailers. `rm -rf release` before `bun test`; no concurrent `bun test`.
- **A Bash timeout shorter than the test-mutex queue leaves a stale lock** (measured 2026-08-24, P2.27): a 2-minute tool timeout killed a run while it was still QUEUED on the mutex, so the lock dir outlived the process that made it and every other lane waited on a dead holder. Diagnose with `ps` (no live `bun test` + a lock dir older than the run) before removing one. With several lanes testing, give a mutex-guarded run a timeout longer than the queue, and always release in a trap rather than only on the success path.
- **A stubbed turn that omits `managed.capabilityLeaseId` silently skips the ENTIRE post-turn cleanup block** (measured 2026-08-24, P3.19): a rig whose `createCapabilityTurn` stub left that field out ran a turn that looked complete and **returned the answer the hypothesis wanted**, while the real code path under test never executed — and the clean-turn positive control did NOT expose it, because a clean turn takes the same shortened path. Any rig that stubs turn creation must assert the cleanup block ran, not merely that the turn resolved.
- **A wrapped clause hides from a phrase grep** (measured 2026-08-24, P2.23's review): when a sentence in a comment or test name wraps across a line break, `grep 'the whole phrase'` misses it while a multiline pattern finds it. P2.23 corrected a false docblock sentence and swept for its citations honestly — and still left a near-verbatim TWIN of that sentence alive in a test name, because the clause wrapped. When you correct a load-bearing sentence, sweep with a MULTILINE pattern (or normalise whitespace first), not a phrase grep, or the copy you leave behind will outlive the one you fixed.
- **NEVER `git commit --amend` in this shared tree** (measured trap, 2026-08-24): the P2.27 lane amended between its own `git add` and its commit, which REWROTE another lane's commit SHA (`fee649d68` → `dc538feb9`) and swept 20 lines of P2.27's test file into P2.6's commit. Nothing was lost, but a review package built on the pre-amend SHA pointed at an object no longer in history, and the controller had already handed that path to a reviewer. Amending rewrites history other lanes and the controller are already referencing. Add commits; never rewrite them.
- `bun test` runs from the REPO ROOT only — bunfig.toml preloads `isolate-shared-config-dir.ts`; a package-cwd run loses CONFIG_DIR isolation and manufactures failures (measured by P2.93: 4 false fails from `packages/shared`, 856/856 from the root). Never `git stash`/`git reset`/`git checkout --`/`git clean` on the shared tree during parallel waves — one stash swallowed three lanes' in-flight edits (recovered).
